Angioembolisation is selected for ongoing bleeding in a suitable patient; a CT blush alone is not a universal paediatric indication. Persistent instability despite blood or peritonitis requires operative assessment. Nonoperative risks include delayed bleeding, biloma/bile leak, missed bowel injury, urinoma and pseudoaneurysm. Use symptom-directed follow-up and an appropriate activity plan.

AAST grading broadly increases from minor capsular haematoma/laceration (I/II), deeper injury (III), major parenchymal/segmental vascular injury (IV), to shattered organ/hilar or major vascular injury (V); liver also has grade VI avulsion in the historical scale. Exact thresholds and the scale revision must be stated when reproducing a full grading table. Preserve splenic tissue when possible. After splenectomy, prevention of overwhelming infection includes pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib immunisation, appropriate antimicrobial prophylaxis, urgent fever assessment and medical-alert education; timing follows age and immune status.

![Original teaching schematic: trauma. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/trauma.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [APSA updated blunt liver/spleen guidelines (2023 publication)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=37117078)

docs.title: Trauma scores, SCIWORA, burns and compartment syndromes
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Trauma scores, SCIWORA, burns and compartment syndromes

GCS sums eye (1-4), verbal (1-5) and motor (1-6) scores to a maximum of 15; use age-appropriate verbal/motor responses in preverbal children. Record individual components and confounders such as intubation/sedation. PTS evaluates weight, airway, systolic BP, CNS, wounds and fractures, each graded +2/+1/-1, total -6 to +12; a low score identifies major injury risk. ISS squares and sums the highest AIS scores from three different body regions; AIS 6 automatically gives ISS 75. Neither score substitutes for resuscitation.

SCIWORA describes traumatic spinal-cord dysfunction without fracture/malalignment on plain films/CT; MRI can show neural/ligamentous injury. Immobilize, document neurological findings and obtain specialist/MRI assessment; delayed deficits can occur. Birth injuries include cephalohaematoma, subgaleal bleeding, fractures and brachial-plexus injury. Cephalohaematoma is subperiosteal and does not cross sutures; usually observe and monitor anaemia/jaundice, avoiding routine aspiration. Subgaleal haemorrhage crosses sutures and can cause life-threatening blood loss. Erb palsy involves upper plexus, often C5-C6; evaluate associated injury and initiate physiotherapy/specialist follow-up, with surgery for selected persistent deficits.

Burn depth: superficial epidermal, superficial/deep partial-thickness dermal, full-thickness, and deeper tissue injury. Local coagulation/stasis/hyperaemia zones coexist with systemic inflammation, capillary leak and hypermetabolism in major burns. Use Lund-Browder age-adjusted charts in children: head proportion is larger and legs smaller than adults. Do not use an unmodified adult rule of nines in a toddler. Cool appropriately without inducing hypothermia, protect airway, estimate TBSA excluding simple erythema, provide analgesia, titrated resuscitation and wound care; monitor perfusion and urine output. Refer major/special-site/inhalation injuries.

Limb compartment syndrome causes pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch and tense compartments; pulses can remain present. Children may show increasing analgesic need, anxiety and agitation. Release constriction and obtain urgent surgical assessment/fasciotomy when indicated. Pediatric abdominal compartment syndrome combines sustained raised intra-abdominal pressure (commonly above 10 mmHg in the consensus paediatric definition) with new/worsening organ dysfunction. Measure bladder pressure using an age-appropriate standard, decompress stomach/bowel, optimize analgesia and fluid balance, drain suitable collections and perform decompressive surgery for refractory organ-threatening disease. Do not wait for absent pulses or profound collapse.

### Paediatric Trauma Score detail
| Variable | +2 | +1 | -1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | >20 kg | 10-20 kg | <10 kg |
| Airway | Normal | Maintained with assistance | Unmaintainable |
| Systolic BP | >90 mmHg | 50-90 mmHg | <50 mmHg |
| CNS | Awake | Obtunded / loss of consciousness | Coma / unresponsive |
| Fracture | None | Closed | Open / multiple |
| Wound | None | Minor | Major / penetrating |

These are the traditional score categories; use clinical age-adjusted physiology during resuscitation. For the adult general-surgery ACS subpart, the adult consensus threshold is sustained intra-abdominal pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction, rather than the lower paediatric threshold. Rising pressure impairs venous return, ventilation, renal perfusion and bowel circulation; urgent decompression is needed when medical measures fail to reverse organ-threatening physiology.

### Paediatric/neonatal fluids, dehydration and electrolyte emergencies

Separate resuscitation, maintenance, pre-existing deficit and ongoing losses; these are not interchangeable. Estimate dehydration from examination and weight change where available. Deficit (mL) = body weight (kg) x percentage dehydration x 10. A 7-kg infant judged 7% dehydrated has an estimated 490-mL deficit; a 10-kg child at 10% has about 1000 mL, but the clinical estimate is imprecise. Severe peritonitis adds third-space losses, sepsis and possible haemorrhage. Use measured clinical response and serial chemistry to refine the plan.

For older infants/children, a common maintenance calculation is 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 for the next 10, and 20 thereafter (the approximate hourly 4-2-1 rule). Neonatal needs differ with age, gestation, humidity, renal function and weight change. Typical term-neonate starting ranges rise from approximately 60-80 mL/kg/day on day 1 to 80-100 on day 2 and 100-120 on day 3; these are starting estimates, not fixed prescriptions for a sick surgical neonate. Prematurity, exposed bowel, phototherapy and losses change requirements. Use glucose-containing maintenance, introduce sodium/potassium according to adaptation, labs and urine output, and avoid blindly applying adult maintenance to neonates.

Shock requires isotonic resuscitation aliquots with frequent perfusion/lung/liver reassessment; choose blood early for haemorrhage. Fluid responsiveness and risk of overload determine further treatment. Replace NG/stoma/urinary losses by measured volume/composition and follow weight, balance, BP, capillary refill, glucose, sodium/potassium/chloride, gases and renal function. Correct hypernatraemic dehydration slowly under close monitoring; avoid rapid osmotic changes. Potassium is added only after renal function/urine output and serum potassium are assessed.

Hyperkalaemia: exclude haemolysed sampling if clinically safe, obtain ECG and assess renal failure, tissue injury, drugs and adrenal disease. Significant ECG changes/severe elevation need monitored IV calcium for membrane protection, insulin with glucose and selected beta-agonist to shift potassium, while stopping potassium input and correcting cause; dialysis may be needed for refractory renal failure. Calcium does not remove potassium. Hypocalcaemia requires ionised calcium interpretation, assessment of magnesium/phosphate and monitored calcium replacement if symptomatic; avoid extravasation and incompatible infusions. State age/weight units explicitly when using a local neonatal emergency-dose protocol.

docs.title: Intestinal failure, nutrition and transplantation
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Intestinal failure, nutrition and transplantation

Short-bowel syndrome is malabsorption after loss of functional small intestine; intestinal failure is inability to maintain adequate nutrition/hydration without parenteral support. Residual length must be interpreted with gestational age, bowel segment, colon continuity, ileocaecal valve and adaptation; a universal length cutoff is misleading. Causes include NEC, volvulus, atresia and gastroschisis. Loss of ileum affects bile-acid/B12 absorption; colon can salvage fluid and carbohydrate energy.

Early care replaces measured fluid/electrolyte losses, gives individualized PN and introduces enteral nutrition as tolerated to stimulate adaptation. Protect central access, avoid overfeeding and monitor triglycerides, glucose, micronutrients and liver function. Treat bacterial overgrowth and specific malabsorption; use acid suppression in selected early hypersecretory states and antimotility treatment when appropriate. Intestinal rehabilitation coordinates surgery, gastroenterology, nutrition and nursing. GLP-2 analogues are selected specialist therapy subject to age/approval and careful monitoring.

Surgery first corrects obstruction, restores continuity and preserves bowel. STEP and longitudinal intestinal lengthening/tailoring (Bianchi) may improve a suitably dilated bowel with persistent dysfunction; neither creates new mucosal mass, and both risk leak, ischaemia and recurrent dilatation. Assess length, vascular pattern, diameter and liver disease before selecting an operation.

Transplant consideration is driven by failure/serious complications of rehabilitation and PN, including progressive intestinal-failure-associated liver disease, threatened loss of central access and recurrent life-threatening catheter sepsis. Assess anatomy, liver/renal function, thrombosis, infections, nutritional status, cardiopulmonary fitness, psychosocial support and immunology. Types include isolated intestine, combined liver-intestine and multivisceral grafts, with modified multivisceral variants. Implant vascular inflow/outflow and intestinal continuity, often with a monitoring access/stoma; immunosuppression and repeated rejection surveillance are essential. Rejection, infection, graft-versus-host disease, PTLD and vascular complications affect outcomes. Long-term PN dependence alone is not an automatic transplant indication.

### Paediatric kidney/liver transplantation and immunosuppression

Kidney-transplant candidates have irreversible kidney failure and acceptable overall fitness; select pre-emptive transplantation where feasible. Evaluate cause of failure/recurrence risk, urine drainage and bladder pressures, infection, vaccines, cardiovascular/nutritional status, vascular anatomy, sensitisation/HLA compatibility and adherence/support. A hostile bladder must be made safe before or with transplantation. Living-related/unrelated and deceased-donor grafts have different logistical/ischaemic considerations; small recipients require careful vascular planning, perfusion and fluid management.

Liver indications include decompensated chronic disease, BA with failed native-liver course, acute liver failure, selected metabolic conditions and selected unresectable tumours. Grafts can be whole deceased-donor, reduced/split or living-donor segmental grafts. The left lateral segments II/III are common for smaller children; a full left lobe includes IV. Assess graft-to-recipient size, vascular/biliary variants and donor safety. Living-donor procurement requires anatomical imaging, mobilization, identification of inflow/outflow and duct, parenchymal transection with adequate donor remnant, and controlled division/reconstruction. Split liver usually produces a left lateral graft for a child and a right-sided graft for another recipient; precise variant and vascular division planning matter.

Small-child challenges include size mismatch, hepatic-artery/portal thrombosis, limited abdominal capacity and variable venous drainage. Use meticulous microsurgical vascular technique, appropriate graft selection and surveillance Doppler. Postoperative care balances perfusion and fluid overload, immunosuppression, infection control, nutrition and rejection assessment. Complications include vascular thrombosis, bile leak/stricture, rejection, infection and PTLD. Prognosis depends on indication, recipient/graft factors and centre practice; avoid an unqualified universal survival percentage.

Immunosuppressants: calcineurin inhibitors tacrolimus/ciclosporin block T-cell activation (nephrotoxicity, hypertension and metabolic/neurotoxicity); steroids have broad anti-inflammatory effects (growth/metabolic/infection risks); mycophenolate inhibits purine synthesis (marrow/GI toxicity, teratogenicity); azathioprine is a purine antimetabolite (marrow/hepatic toxicity); mTOR inhibitors inhibit proliferation (wound, lipid and marrow effects). Induction may use anti-IL2-receptor or lymphocyte-depleting agents. Drug choice/levels are organ- and protocol-specific. Surveillance includes trough levels, organ function, viral disease, malignancy risk and lifelong adherence/transition support.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NIDDK: Kidney transplantation](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/kidney-failure/kidney-transplant)
- [NCI PDQ: Childhood liver cancer, professional version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/liver/hp/child-liver-treatment-pdq?cid=eb_govdel_esp)

docs.title: Germ-cell tumours, sacrococcygeal teratoma and testis preservation
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Germ-cell tumours, sacrococcygeal teratoma and testis preservation

Germ-cell tumours derive from primordial germ cells with gonadal or midline extragonadal sites. Histological types include mature/immature teratoma, yolk-sac (endodermal-sinus) tumour, seminomatous tumours, embryonal carcinoma and choriocarcinoma, often mixed. AFP supports yolk-sac differentiation and monitoring; beta-hCG supports trophoblastic components; LDH reflects burden in selected tumours. Interpret AFP against age because infants normally have high AFP. Failure of a marker to decline appropriately after treatment suggests residual disease, but use known biological half-life and age norms.

SCT Altman types: I predominantly external; II external with significant intrapelvic extension; III predominantly pelvic/abdominal with an external component; IV entirely presacral. Approximate historical distributions are about 45%, 35%, 10% and 10%, varying by series. Fetal prognosis depends on solid vascular mass, high-output failure, hydrops, tumour growth, prematurity and bleeding, rather than type alone. Ultrasound/echo and selected MRI guide monitoring and delivery. Surgical excision includes the coccyx, preserving pelvic nerves and sphincter function. Resect without spillage where feasible; malignant elements require oncology input. Follow serial age-adjusted AFP, imaging/clinical recurrence, continence and bowel/urinary function. Immature histology is not identical to malignant yolk-sac tumour.

Testicular masses need ultrasound and preoperative AFP/beta-hCG; assess puberty/age and metastatic staging according to pathology. A suspected malignant tumour generally requires inguinal exploration with cord control, avoiding transscrotal biopsy. Testis-sparing excision is considered for suitable prepubertal likely benign lesions when normal tissue can be preserved and reliable frozen/permanent pathology is available. Malignant germ-cell tumour commonly requires radical inguinal orchidectomy and protocol-specific chemotherapy/staging. Staging distinguishes disease confined to the gonad, retroperitoneal spread and distant metastases, but specify the paediatric protocol rather than importing adult staging uncritically.

Yolk-sac tumour shows AFP secretion, characteristic reticular morphology and possible Schiller-Duval bodies. Counsel about fertility/endocrine function and surveillance. Never infer a tumour is benign solely because it is painless or an ultrasound is cystic.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NCI PDQ: Childhood extracranial germ-cell tumours, professional version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/extracranial-germ-cell/hp/germ-cell-treatment-pdq)

docs.title: Research designs, statistics, bias and publication metrics
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Research designs, statistics, bias and publication metrics

Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at one time: useful for prevalence (e.g. constipation in a clinic), but limited for temporal causality. Case-control studies start with an outcome and compare past exposures (e.g. surgical infection cases and controls); efficient for rare outcomes, but vulnerable to recall/selection bias and usually estimate an odds ratio. Cohorts start with exposure and follow outcomes (e.g. two repair techniques and later fistula); they estimate incidence and relative risk. A retrospective cohort reconstructs follow-up from existing records, preserving the exposure-to-outcome logic despite retrospective data collection.

An RCT specifies a focused PICO question, eligibility, outcomes, sample-size plan and ethics/registration; obtains consent; uses an unpredictable random sequence and concealed allocation; implements treatment; masks relevant participants/assessors when feasible; follows losses/adherence; and analyses with a prespecified plan, typically intention to treat. Randomisation balances confounders on average, but small trials can retain imbalance. Allocation concealment prevents selective enrolment; blinding reduces performance/detection bias. Advantages include stronger causal inference; disadvantages include cost, feasibility, ethical constraints, crossover, imperfect generalisability and difficulty masking operations. Hierarchies favour high-quality systematic reviews/RCTs for intervention questions but appropriate designs differ for diagnosis, prognosis and rare harm.

Reduce bias with representative recruitment, comparable groups, valid blinded measurement, concealed allocation, prospectively defined outcomes, complete follow-up and adjustment for measured confounding where appropriate. Formulate FINER (feasible, interesting, novel, ethical, relevant) and PICO questions; predefine a clinically important effect rather than choose a sample to produce significance.

For a single proportion, n is approximately Z² p(1-p)/d²; specify desired precision d and plausible p. For comparing groups, use an appropriate formula/software with expected effect, variance/event rate, alpha, power, allocation and allowances for attrition/clustering. A p value is the probability, assuming the null model, of results at least as incompatible with that model as observed. It is not the probability the null is true and does not measure clinical importance. Report effect size and confidence intervals.

Relative risk compares outcome risks in exposed/unexposed groups; odds ratio compares odds and approximates RR only when the outcome is uncommon. Diagnostic sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN); specificity = TN/(TN+FP); PPV = TP/(TP+FP); NPV = TN/(TN+FN); positive likelihood ratio = sensitivity/(1-specificity), negative LR = (1-sensitivity)/specificity. PPV/NPV change with prevalence; sensitivity/specificity can also vary with case spectrum. Avoid 'accuracy' alone for an imbalanced dataset.

A systematic review uses a prespecified question, reproducible search, eligibility, appraisal and synthesis; meta-analysis is statistical pooling and may be inappropriate with incompatible studies. PRISMA is a reporting framework with checklist/flow diagram, not a certificate that a review is unbiased. Clinical audit compares practice against an explicit standard, implements improvement and reaudits; research asks a question to generate knowledge. A journal impact factor broadly relates citations in a year to recent citable items; it is a journal-level metric, not quality proof for an individual paper. Citation counts, h-index and indexing are different. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science have different functions/coverage; MEDLINE selection is not identical to simply appearing in PubMed.

docs.title: Neonatal sepsis, legacy SIRS and MODS
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Neonatal sepsis, legacy SIRS and MODS

Neonatal infection risks include prematurity, maternal infection, prolonged membrane rupture, invasive devices, operations, poor barriers and prolonged hospitalization. Early-onset pathogens are often maternally acquired, while late-onset organisms reflect community or unit microbiology. Symptoms can be subtle: temperature instability, apnoea, feeding difficulty, lethargy, glucose instability and poor perfusion. Obtain cultures and appropriate laboratory assessment promptly, but treat shock without waiting for confirmatory results. Empiric agents depend on onset, source and local resistance; reassess and narrow when microbiology is known. Source control includes infected devices and surgical infection.

For historical questions, paediatric SIRS requires at least two of abnormal core temperature (>38.5 or <36 degrees C), age-inappropriate heart rate (including bradycardia in infants), increased respiratory rate/acute ventilatory need, and abnormal age-adjusted WBC or >10% immature forms; one must be temperature or WBC. Pain, anaesthesia and treatment-related leucopenia need interpretation. SIRS is nonspecific and not the modern sole definition of sepsis.

Current paediatric consensus uses suspected infection with life-threatening organ dysfunction; the Phoenix criteria apply to the defined paediatric population and are not a universal neonatal-screening tool. Recognise respiratory, cardiovascular, neurological and coagulation dysfunction clinically and initiate therapy early rather than wait for a score to accumulate. MODS is dysfunction of multiple organ systems requiring intervention to maintain homeostasis. Inflammation, endothelial injury, microvascular dysregulation and immune dysfunction interact to produce tissue hypoxia and organ failure.

Management supports oxygenation/perfusion, glucose/electrolytes and temperature, gives timely antimicrobials and source control, and uses vasoactive support when fluid responsiveness is exhausted or overload is developing. Monitor lactate trend, urine output, mental state and evolving organs. Scleroderma is a distinct connective-tissue disease with skin sclerosis and possible systemic vascular/organ disease; do not silently substitute the neonatal term 'sclerema' when the source explicitly says scleroderma. If sclerema was intended, it describes diffuse hardening of subcutaneous tissue in severely ill neonates and demands treatment of underlying critical illness. Flag that terminology ambiguity for faculty clarification.

### Organ-by-organ MODS assessment
Assess respiratory failure, myocardial/perfusion dysfunction, oliguria/acute kidney injury, hepatic synthetic dysfunction, thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy and altered neurological function. Track support requirements as well as abnormal tests: a ventilated, vasopressor-dependent child can have evolving dysfunction despite initially reassuring individual values. Management includes source control, oxygen delivery, nutrition, prevention of secondary device infections and appropriate organ support, with renal replacement for indicated severe renal/metabolic failure. Scores can standardize reporting but do not replace bedside reassessment.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [International paediatric sepsis consensus: Phoenix (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10900966/)
- [Original 2005 International Pediatric Sepsis Consensus](https://sepsis-one.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/Consenso-Sepsis-en-Pediatria.pdf)

docs.title: Lung development, CPAM, sequestration and lobar resection
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Lung development, CPAM, sequestration and lobar resection

### Development and classification
The respiratory diverticulum arises from ventral foregut endoderm; surrounding splanchnic mesoderm forms supporting tissue. Stages are embryonic, pseudoglandular (roughly 5-17 weeks), canalicular (16-26 weeks), saccular (24 weeks to birth) and alveolar (late fetal life through childhood). CPAM is abnormal airway branching/maturation; the older name CCAM should be identified but updated in the answer.

Stocker types: 0, proximal acinar dysplasia; 1, large cysts; 2, multiple smaller cysts and more associated anomalies; 3, microcystic/solid appearing lesions; 4, large peripheral thin-walled cysts. Prenatal imaging also uses macrocystic versus microcystic appearance. Pulmonary sequestration is dysplastic tissue without normal bronchial communication supplied by a systemic artery, usually from the aorta. Intralobar sequestration shares visceral pleura with the adjacent lung; extralobar sequestration has separate pleura and more associated anomalies. Hybrid CPAM/sequestration lesions occur.

### Antenatal and postnatal management
Serial ultrasound documents lesion size, CPAM volume ratio (CVR = length x width x height x 0.52/head circumference), mediastinal shift, hydrops, dominant cyst and systemic supply. A CVR above about 1.6 is a commonly used risk indicator, not a solitary treatment mandate. Assess cardiac compression and fetal growth. Large microcystic lesions with evolving hydrops may be considered for maternal corticosteroids by a fetal team; a dominant macrocyst may be drained with a thoracoamniotic shunt. Selected refractory disease needs specialised fetal intervention. Plan EXIT only when a predicted airway or ventilation problem warrants it.

A distressed neonate needs respiratory support and evaluation for urgent resection. In an asymptomatic infant, cross-sectional contrast imaging defines anatomy and feeding vessels; a normal chest radiograph does not exclude the lesion. Elective resection versus surveillance requires discussion of infection, symptoms, diagnostic uncertainty, rare malignancy concerns and anaesthetic/operative risks. Avoid presenting surgery for all asymptomatic lesions as universally agreed.

### Operative anatomy
The right lung has three lobes and the left two, with a lingula in the left upper lobe. Pulmonary arteries accompany bronchi; veins run mainly in intersegmental planes and drain to the left atrium. At the right hilum, the upper-lobe bronchus is eparterial; the right pulmonary artery lies anterior to the main bronchus. The left pulmonary artery arches above the left main bronchus. Understand individual arterial branches, pulmonary venous drainage and fissural variation before division.

For left upper lobectomy: position and isolate ventilation when feasible; inspect the pleura and fissure; identify and control upper-lobe venous drainage while preserving lower-lobe veins; dissect and divide upper-lobe arterial branches including lingular supply; identify/divide the upper-lobe bronchus without compromising the lower-lobe bronchus; complete the fissure, retrieve specimen, test for air leak and place drainage as indicated. Sequestration requires early recognition and secure control of the systemic feeder. Complications include bleeding, air leak, bronchial injury, infection and residual disease.

### Resection indications and lobar anatomy in an examination answer
Indications for paediatric lung resection include symptomatic congenital malformation, sequestration with infection/complications, localised destructive infection/bronchiectasis, selected tumours and refractory local pathology. The right main bronchus branches to upper-lobe bronchus and bronchus intermedius (middle/lower lobes); the left divides into upper/lower lobar bronchi. Identify superior/inferior pulmonary veins separately and recognise anomalous drainage before division. A posterior left hilar view differs from the familiar anterior 'RALS' relation, so state orientation when drawing.

### Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: embryology, prognostication and stabilization

### Development and types
The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum (central tendon), paired pleuroperitoneal folds, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus (crura), and muscular ingrowth from the body wall. Its descent explains the phrenic nerve supply from C3-C5. A simple failure-of-closure account is incomplete: abnormal pleuroperitoneal-fold mesenchyme and disturbed muscle development contribute to the defect; pulmonary hypoplasia may precede and then be aggravated by herniation (dual-hit model).

Bochdalek defects are posterolateral, usually left sided; Morgagni defects are anterior/retrosternal; central tendon defects are uncommon. Eventration is an intact but deficiently muscular diaphragm, rather than a true hole. Distinguish a hiatal hernia through the oesophageal hiatus from CDH. Label the heart, liver, bowel, lung and defect in a schematic.

### Antenatal assessment
Ultrasound shows intrathoracic stomach/bowel, mediastinal shift and a small ipsilateral lung. Assess side, liver position, observed-to-expected lung-to-head ratio (o/e LHR), defect severity, associated cardiac/genetic abnormalities and polyhydramnios. Fetal MRI estimates total fetal lung volume and liver herniation. Large defects, liver up, low o/e LHR or lung volume, and major associated anomalies worsen prognosis. Postnatally, pulmonary hypertension, ventricular dysfunction, oxygen requirement, oxygenation index and ECMO requirement add physiological information. Survival figures must specify whether they describe all diagnosed pregnancies, live births or treated infants.

### Immediate and intensive care management
Plan delivery in a centre with neonatal intensive care and paediatric surgery. Intubate a symptomatic known-CDH neonate and decompress the stomach with an orogastric tube; bag-mask ventilation can inflate intrathoracic bowel. Maintain warmth, analgesia and careful handling. Use gentle pressure-limited ventilation; avoid volutrauma and accept appropriate permissive hypercapnia while following pH, lactate and perfusion. Conventional ventilation is commonly first line; high-frequency ventilation is a rescue option when acceptable gas exchange cannot be obtained within safe pressures. Titrate oxygen to preductal saturation and assess pre/postductal difference. Echocardiography defines pulmonary hypertension and biventricular function; pulmonary vasodilators and vasoactive drugs should follow that physiology, rather than be given automatically.

Give cautious isotonic fluid aliquots with reassessment; excessive fluid worsens pulmonary oedema. Monitor arterial gases, BP, lactate trend, urine output, electrolytes and echocardiography. Refractory cardiopulmonary failure may require ECMO in an eligible infant. Repair follows physiological stabilization, rather than an arbitrary time after birth: acceptable oxygenation/ventilation on stable settings, satisfactory BP and urine output, improving lactate and controlled pulmonary hypertension. Reduce viscera and obtain tension-free closure; use a patch for a large defect. Severe physiology and large defects favour open repair; selected stable infants may undergo minimally invasive repair.

### Sudden acidosis and long-term issues
Check displaced/blocked tube, pneumothorax, worsening pulmonary hypertension, ventricular failure, sepsis, inadequate perfusion and bowel compromise. Check the circuit and tube, examine, obtain bedside imaging/echo and correct the cause promptly. Follow recurrence, pulmonary disease, reflux, growth, hearing and neurodevelopment. The historical shift is from urgent anatomical repair to lung-protective stabilization and delayed repair. FETO is a specialised option for selected severe fetal CDH, with prematurity and balloon-removal risks; it is not routine treatment for every fetus.

### Lung pathology and the management implication
Affected lungs have fewer/smaller airways and alveolar units and a reduced pulmonary vascular bed. Abnormal vascular muscularisation/reactivity contributes to high pulmonary vascular resistance, with right-heart pressure load and possible left-ventricular dysfunction. Consequently, high-pressure ventilation cannot simply 'inflate the missing lung'; overdistension of relatively preserved lung worsens injury and haemodynamics. Gentle ventilation, echocardiography-directed circulation support and delayed repair address this physiological disease alongside the anatomical defect.

![Original teaching schematic: cdh development. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/cdh-development.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [ERNICA guidelines and endorsed statements](https://www.ern-ernica.eu/guidelines)
- [Canadian CDH Collaborative 2023 guideline update](https://fn.bmj.com/content/109/3/239)

docs.title: Hirschsprung disease: diagnosis, pull-through and postoperative obstruction
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Hirschsprung disease: diagnosis, pull-through and postoperative obstruction

### Pathogenesis, genetics and diagnosis
Failure of neural-crest-derived enteric cells to populate distal bowel produces contiguous distal aganglionosis of submucosal and myenteric plexuses. The affected segment fails to relax, with proximal dilatation. RET-pathway abnormalities are central; EDNRB, EDN3, SOX10 and other genes contribute. Associations include Down syndrome, Waardenburg-Shah syndrome and Mowat-Wilson syndrome. Genetic counselling is especially relevant in familial, syndromic and long-segment disease.

Presentations include delayed meconium, neonatal obstruction, enterocolitis, failure to thrive or childhood constipation. Rectal examination may produce explosive stool but is neither necessary nor confirmatory. Contrast enema can show a transition zone, reversed rectosigmoid ratio and delayed evacuation; it may be misleading in neonates and total colonic disease. Anorectal manometry demonstrates an absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR), but histology establishes the diagnosis.

Take adequate rectal suction biopsies above the physiologically hypoganglionic anal zone, with sufficient submucosa; a full-thickness biopsy is used when suction tissue is inadequate or results conflict. H&E assesses absent ganglion cells and hypertrophic nerves. Increased acetylcholinesterase activity supports diagnosis; absent mucosal/submucosal calretinin staining is useful. Interpret with specimen quality, age and expert pathology. Intraoperative biopsies must demonstrate ganglionated bowel clear of the transition zone.

### Definitive operation
Decompress with rectal irrigations, correct sepsis/nutrition and map the disease. Selected stable, decompressed rectosigmoid cases can have a single-stage transanal endorectal pull-through; diversion is appropriate for instability, severe enterocolitis, difficult decompression or extensive disease. Swenson removes the aganglionic rectum with a low anastomosis; Soave pulls ganglionated bowel through an endorectal muscular cuff; Duhamel creates a retrorectal pull-through and joins it to the retained anterior rectum. Preserve sphincters and dentate-line sensation; avoid twist, tension, ischaemia and a restrictive cuff.

Total colonic aganglionosis requires serial biopsies including small bowel; imaging alone cannot define its proximal extent. Emergency diversion must be placed in proven ganglionated bowel. Definitive ileoanal pull-through options include straight/Soave-type or modified Duhamel reconstruction, chosen with nutritional and continence implications. Follow hydration, growth, sodium loss, skin injury and enterocolitis. “Ultra-short segment” disease is controversial: distinguish internal anal sphincter achalasia (absent RAIR with ganglion cells) and functional constipation before proposing resection.

### Persistent symptoms after surgery
First distinguish true incontinence from overflow due to obstruction. Obtain operative/histology records, examination under anaesthesia, contrast enema, and repeat biopsy when indicated. Mechanical causes include stricture, twisted pull-through, retained Soave cuff or Duhamel spur; histological causes include transition-zone pull-through/residual aganglionosis. Functional causes include internal sphincter achalasia and dysmotility. Treat demonstrable structural disease appropriately; use irrigations, a structured bowel regimen and selected botulinum toxin injection for outlet dysfunction. Redo surgery needs a defined cause and experienced team. Long-term surveillance covers continence, constipation, HAEC, psychosocial health and transition to adult care.

### Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis

HAEC is an inflammatory syndrome related to dysbiosis, mucosal barrier impairment, immune dysfunction and bowel stasis; it occurs before or after pull-through. Long-segment disease, Down syndrome, prior HAEC and persistent obstruction increase risk. Presentations range from foul diarrhoea, distension and fever to ileus, shock, lethargy and perforation; diarrhoea does not exclude obstructed bowel.

A useful clinical grading is possible/mild HAEC (grade I), definite HAEC (grade II) and severe HAEC (grade III with systemic instability or severe abdominal findings). A formal HAEC score may help research or documentation but must not delay treatment. Plain radiographs identify dilatation, ileus, pneumatosis or perforation. Check CBC, electrolytes, acid-base status and cultures where clinically indicated. Avoid a contrast enema during acute severe enterocolitis because of perforation risk.

Mild disease may respond to close supervision, hydration, oral metronidazole and saline rectal irrigations in an appropriate patient. Definite disease generally requires admission, bowel rest, IV fluids, broad antimicrobial cover including anaerobes, frequent irrigations and gastric decompression when vomiting/distended. Severe disease requires intensive care resuscitation, correction of electrolytes/coagulopathy and urgent surgical review. Perforation or refractory obstruction may require diversion. Irrigations remove retained faecal material; they are not simply small-volume enemas.

After recovery investigate recurrent disease for stricture, restrictive cuff, retained spur, twist or residual aganglionosis. Ensure caregivers can recognise early warning symptoms and perform prescribed irrigations. Probiotics and routine long-term antibiotics have inconsistent evidence and should not replace relief of obstruction. An exam answer should explicitly show the sequence: recognise -> resuscitate -> decompress -> antibiotics -> identify/treat precipitating obstruction.

docs.title: Appendicitis and intussusception
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Appendicitis and intussusception

Appendicitis can cause perforation, abscess, phlegmon, peritonitis, sepsis and bowel obstruction. Assess migration/localisation of pain, anorexia, vomiting, fever and examination; combine inflammatory tests with ultrasound first where available. CT/MRI is selected for unresolved diagnostic uncertainty. PAS, Alvarado and paediatric appendicitis risk calculators support risk stratification but do not replace clinical judgement. Treat with analgesia, fluids, antibiotics and timely appendicectomy when indicated. Antibiotics-first treatment in carefully selected uncomplicated disease may avoid initial surgery but has failure/recurrence risks; a faecolith, complication or unreliable follow-up changes suitability. Established abscess/phlegmon may be managed initially with antibiotics and selected image-guided drainage.

Intussusception is telescoping of bowel: the intussusceptum has entering and returning layers within the receiving intussuscipiens, dragging mesentery and causing venous congestion, ischaemia and eventually perforation. Most infant ileocolic cases have no discrete lead point; Meckel diverticulum, duplication, polyp, lymphoma and postoperative abnormalities become more important in older/recurrent patients. Intermittent pain, vomiting, lethargy and late bloody stool occur; the full classic triad is often absent. Ultrasound target/doughnut and longitudinal pseudokidney signs establish diagnosis.

Resuscitate, decompress if required and obtain surgical support. A stable child without peritonitis/perforation is eligible for image-guided pneumatic reduction or hydrostatic saline/contrast reduction. Prerequisites include monitored pressure, trained radiology staff, resuscitation equipment and immediate access to surgery. Air is efficient but involves radiation if fluoroscopic; ultrasound-guided saline avoids radiation but is operator dependent. Perforation, peritonitis and instability contraindicate attempted enema reduction. Failure, pathological lead point or complications requires laparoscopy/laparotomy with gentle reduction and resection of nonviable bowel. A prolapsed intussusceptum may allow a sulcus between protruding bowel and anal wall, whereas rectal prolapse is continuous with the anal mucosa; an ill child with obstruction must not be managed as simple prolapse.


### Contemporary appendicitis evidence
A 2025 paediatric trial found higher one-year treatment failure with antibiotics (34%) than appendicectomy (7%); failure definitions differed by arm. This strengthens counselling about initial avoidance of surgery and later intervention.

![Original teaching schematic: intussusception. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/intussusception.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [2025 paediatric appendicectomy versus antibiotics randomized trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39826968/)
- [Lancet original appendicitis trial (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673624024206)

docs.title: Intestinal, colonic and pyloric atresia
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Intestinal, colonic and pyloric atresia

Duodenal atresia is classically associated with disordered recanalisation, Down syndrome and annular pancreas. Jejunoileal atresia is commonly attributed to an intrauterine vascular insult. Jejunoileal types are I (mucosal web), II (blind ends connected by a cord), IIIa (mesenteric gap), IIIb (apple-peel configuration) and IV (multiple atresias). Duodenal obstruction may be complete or a stenosis/web; differentiate malrotation with volvulus.

Prenatal ultrasound may show polyhydramnios, double bubble or dilated bowel. Postnatally assess bilious vomiting, distension and failure of stool; plain films define gas distribution. A double bubble without distal gas supports complete duodenal obstruction, whereas distal gas does not exclude a partial web or malrotation. In distal obstruction, contrast enema can demonstrate microcolon and localise colonic obstruction. Examine for associated cardiac and other anomalies.

Resuscitate and decompress before surgery. Duodenoduodenostomy bypasses duodenal atresia/annular obstruction while respecting the ampulla. For jejunoileal disease, inspect the full bowel for additional atresias, resect a short dysfunctional proximal segment when appropriate, preserve maximal length and create a well-perfused, tension-free anastomosis. Tapering enteroplasty may improve a markedly dilated proximal bowel when extensive resection would threaten length. Multiple atresias may require several anastomoses, selective tapering or diversion according to stability, perfusion and bowel length. Colonic atresia usually needs resection/anastomosis or staged diversion; consider distal aganglionosis before restoring continuity.

Pyloric atresia may be a membrane, solid cord or separated ends and can associate with epidermolysis bullosa. Distinguish it from IHPS; treatment may be membrane excision/pyloroplasty or gastroduodenostomy according to anatomy. Segmental bowel dilatation is a sharply localised dilated segment with relatively normal proximal/distal bowel; exclude mechanical obstruction and dysmotility before resection. Prognosis after any atresia depends on prematurity, associated abnormalities, sepsis, bowel length, dysmotility and intestinal-failure complications. Postoperative care includes gastric decompression, PN when required, gradual enteral feeds and growth monitoring.

### Neonatal hypoglycaemia and congenital hyperinsulinism

Neonatal hypoglycaemia thresholds depend on age, symptoms and risk; operational treatment thresholds in transitional newborn care are not identical to diagnostic criteria for a persistent disorder. Screen risk groups, measure glucose with laboratory confirmation of a low bedside result when feasible, and treat symptomatic low glucose immediately. Symptoms include jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, apnoea and seizures; some infants are asymptomatic. Causes include prematurity, growth restriction, maternal diabetes, sepsis, endocrine deficiencies and metabolic disease.

Prevent prolonged fasting, monitor perioperative glucose and maintain an appropriate glucose infusion. Symptomatic or severe episodes generally require IV dextrose and a continuous infusion titrated to frequent values; small asymptomatic transitional episodes may be managed with feeding and selected dextrose gel according to neonatal protocol. Calculate glucose infusion rate (mg/kg/min) from concentration and infusion rate rather than giving an unlabelled 'percentage'. A 10% solution contains 100 mg/mL; GIR = 100 x mL/hour divided by 60 x weight (kg). Avoid abrupt withdrawal after prolonged high glucose delivery.

Persistent/recurrent disease requires a critical sample during hypoglycaemia, if safe: plasma glucose, insulin/C-peptide, ketones, free fatty acids, cortisol, growth hormone and selected lactate/ammonia/metabolic tests. Congenital hyperinsulinism ('nesidioblastosis' is historical and not a complete modern classification) shows inappropriate insulin action with suppressed ketones/free fatty acids, high glucose requirement and a glycaemic response to glucagon. Focal and diffuse forms have different genetics and operative options. ABCC8/KCNJ11 and other variants guide assessment; 18F-DOPA PET can localise focal disease in appropriate centres.

Management includes continuous reliable glucose supply, selected glucagon, diazoxide responsiveness assessment and monitoring of adverse effects, with other agents under endocrine care. A focal lesion may be cured by limited resection; diffuse refractory disease may need extensive pancreatic surgery but risks later diabetes and exocrine insufficiency. Protect neurodevelopment by preventing repeated episodes. The biochemical diagnosis and molecular/localisation plan should precede an indiscriminate near-total pancreatectomy.

### Intestinal rotation, malrotation and midgut volvulus

The midgut elongates, herniates physiologically into the umbilical cord around week 6 and rotates approximately 270 degrees counterclockwise around the SMA, viewed from the front, during herniation and return around week 10. Subsequent fixation places the duodenojejunal junction left of the spine and the caecum in the right lower quadrant, producing a broad mesenteric base. Nonrotation, incomplete rotation and abnormal fixation leave a narrow base and obstructing peritoneal bands; reversed rotation and internal hernia variants occur.

Bilious vomiting in a neonate demands urgent exclusion of volvulus. Older children may have intermittent pain/vomiting, poor growth or acute ischaemia. Stable patients usually undergo an upper-GI contrast study to locate the duodenojejunal junction and identify a corkscrew appearance. Ultrasound may show abnormal SMA/SMV relation and a whirlpool of mesentery/SMV around the SMA; vessel inversion alone is not definitive. In shock, peritonitis or strong evidence of ischaemic volvulus, resuscitation and surgery must not be delayed for a complete imaging sequence.

Keep nil by mouth; decompress stomach, obtain IV/IO access, restore perfusion, administer antibiotics for suspected ischaemia, and monitor lactate/electrolytes. At operation inspect viability, detorse the usual clockwise volvulus counterclockwise, divide Ladd bands, mobilise the duodenum/right colon and broaden the mesenteric base. Place small bowel predominantly on the right and colon on the left; appendicectomy is commonly performed because the caecum remains ectopic. The Ladd procedure does not restore normal embryological rotation. Reassess questionable bowel after reperfusion; preserve length and consider a planned second look rather than aggressive removal of potentially recoverable intestine.

Laparoscopy is feasible for stable selected cases, but gross distension, suspected ischaemia or instability may favour open surgery. Ensure mesenteric broadening is adequate. Long-term problems include adhesive obstruction, rare recurrent volvulus, persistent symptoms and short bowel after extensive resection. Families should seek immediate assessment for recurrent bilious vomiting.

### Neonatal cholestasis, biliary atresia and Kasai outcomes

### Recognition and investigation
Conjugated jaundice is pathological. Persistent jaundice, pale/acholic stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly warrant prompt direct bilirubin measurement and hepatobiliary assessment. A direct bilirubin above 1 mg/dL is an important abnormal threshold; the older requirement that it exceed 20% of total bilirubin can miss disease. Differential diagnosis includes biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, infection, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Alagille syndrome, metabolic/endocrine disorders, genetic bile-transport disease and parenteral-nutrition-associated cholestasis.

Assess stool colour, growth, bleeding and splenic/associated abnormalities. Tests include fractionated bilirubin, liver enzymes/GGT, albumin, glucose, INR (including response to vitamin K), CBC, cultures when needed and targeted metabolic/genetic investigations. Fasting ultrasound assesses gallbladder morphology, triangular-cord sign, ducts, cysts and vascular anatomy. No single negative ultrasound or scintigraphic result reliably excludes BA. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy can demonstrate excretion; absent excretion is nonspecific and must not delay definitive evaluation. Liver biopsy often shows bile duct proliferation, bile plugs, portal oedema and fibrosis. Intraoperative cholangiography establishes extrahepatic patency/anatomy when BA is suspected.

### Pathology and operation
BA is progressive fibro-obliterative cholangiopathy with interacting developmental, inflammatory and immune mechanisms. CMV-associated BA is a described subgroup; association does not prove CMV causes all BA, and antiviral treatment needs specialist selection. Anatomical types are I (common bile duct), II (common hepatic duct, with subtypes), and III (at porta hepatis; most common). A cystic hilar lesion may represent cystic BA rather than a patent choledochal cyst; assess distal patency and hepatic ducts.

Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy removes the fibrotic extrahepatic remnant and exposes microscopic ductules at the portal plate, connected to a Roux-en-Y jejunal limb. Earlier diagnosis and surgery improve the chance of bile drainage; age is not the sole criterion. Avoid damage to portal vessels and inappropriate deep excision. Provide high-energy nutrition, fat-soluble vitamins, cholangitis treatment and surveillance. The benefit of routine steroids is unsettled and protocol dependent.

### Prognosis and transplantation
Jaundice clearance and bilirubin after Kasai, age/fibrosis at operation, anatomical/syndromic disease, recurrent cholangitis, centre experience and portal hypertension influence native-liver survival. Some children retain native liver long term, while others develop cirrhosis despite initial bile drainage. Follow growth, fat-soluble vitamins, coagulopathy, varices, ascites, hepatopulmonary syndrome and malignancy surveillance where indicated. Refer early for transplant assessment after failed drainage, progressive decompensation, refractory portal-hypertension complications, severe growth failure or recurrent uncontrollable cholangitis. Kasai is a bridge to long-term native-liver health or transplantation, rather than a guaranteed cure.

![Original teaching schematic: malrotation. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/malrotation.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN infant cholestasis guideline](https://www.naspghan.org/files/documents/pdfs/position-papers/Guideline_for_the_Evaluation_of_Cholestatic.23.pdf)

docs.title: Pharyngeal arches: exam table of nerves, muscles and arteries
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Pharyngeal arches: exam table of nerves, muscles and arteries

| Arch | Principal skeletal/muscular derivatives | Nerve | Classic arterial remnant |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Malleus/incus and jaw-associated structures; mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani/veli palatini | Trigeminal, especially V3 for muscle | Part of maxillary artery |
| 2 | Stapes, styloid/stylohyoid, lesser hyoid horn/upper body; facial expression, stapedius, posterior digastric | VII | Mostly regresses; transient hyoid/stapedial arteries |
| 3 | Greater hyoid horn/lower body; stylopharyngeus | IX | Common carotid and proximal internal carotid |
| 4 | Contribution to laryngeal framework; pharyngeal constrictors, cricothyroid, levator veli palatini | X, superior laryngeal | Left aortic-arch portion, right proximal subclavian |
| 5 | No standard durable adult derivative in traditional numbering | None assigned | Absent/rudimentary in traditional scheme |
| 6 | Laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid; laryngeal-framework contribution | X, recurrent laryngeal | Proximal pulmonary arteries; left distal part becomes ductus arteriosus |

Pouches and clefts must be tabulated separately from arches: first pouch middle ear/auditory tube; second tonsillar epithelium; third thymus/inferior parathyroids; fourth superior parathyroids/ultimobranchial contribution. The external auditory canal is the first cleft; other clefts normally disappear as the cervical sinus is obliterated. Describe this as the traditional clinical-exam scheme: contemporary embryological nomenclature has debated the literal 'fifth arch'. Avoid conflating an artery remnant with an entire adult vessel.

### Branchial anomalies, thyroglossal tract and cervical lymphadenopathy

The first arch forms jaws/masticatory structures and is supplied by CN V; the second forms stapes/styloid/stylohyoid and upper hyoid components with CN VII; the third forms lower hyoid components with CN IX; fourth/sixth arches contribute laryngeal cartilages/muscles with superior/recurrent laryngeal branches of CN X. The fifth is rudimentary. First pouch forms middle ear/auditory tube; second tonsillar epithelium; third thymus and inferior parathyroids; fourth superior parathyroids and ultimobranchial contribution. First cleft forms external auditory canal; remaining clefts are normally obliterated. First-arch syndromes include mandibulofacial abnormalities; assess airway and hearing.

Second-branchial fistula commonly extends from anterior SCM skin, between carotid branches, towards the tonsillar region; cysts can present as lateral neck swelling. First-cleft anomalies may track through parotid/external ear structures and require facial-nerve protection. Third/fourth pouch sinuses often reach the pyriform fossa and can cause recurrent, often left-sided, thyroid/neck infection; endoscopy and imaging help define them. Treat acute infection first, then excise the tract or perform selected endoscopic closure with protection of nearby nerves/vessels.

Thyroglossal remnants arise along thyroid descent from foramen caecum. Midline swelling moves with swallowing/tongue protrusion; suprahyoid, juxtahyoid and infrahyoid sites occur. Differential includes dermoid, ectopic thyroid, nodes and other cysts. Ultrasound confirms a normal thyroid and characterises the lesion; thyroid-function tests/scintigraphy are selected when ectopic-only thyroid is possible. Sistrunk excision removes cyst/tract, central hyoid and a core of tissue towards the tongue base. Simple cyst excision has high recurrence. Treat infection before elective repair.

Neck nodes: I submental/submandibular; II upper jugular; III middle jugular; IV lower jugular; V posterior triangle; VI central compartment; VII upper mediastinal. Persistent suspicious nodes require history/examination, ultrasound, CBC and targeted infection testing, then tissue sampling suitable for suspected pathology. Avoid corticosteroids before diagnostic sampling of possible lymphoma unless urgently necessary. Sialadenitis evaluation includes hydration, oral/dental findings, ultrasound and duct disease; chronic cases may need sialendoscopy. Do not remove ectopic thyroid without proving adequate alternative functioning thyroid.

### Operative detail for branchial fistula and Sistrunk
For a second-branchial tract, mark the external opening, use a skin-crease/selected step-ladder exposure, follow the tract through its anatomical path and protect hypoglossal/glossopharyngeal nerves and carotid vessels. Excise to the internal termination when safely defined; dye/probes are aids, not substitutes for anatomy. In Sistrunk surgery remove the central hyoid with the cyst and tract en bloc and a core of suprahyoid tissue directed towards the foramen caecum. Recurrence is associated with residual tract, inadequate hyoid/core excision or prior infection. Confirm normal thyroid before excising a possible sole ectopic thyroid.

### First-arch associations
Treacher Collins has mandibulofacial dysostosis with important airway/ear issues; hemifacial microsomia/Goldenhar spectrum involves variable craniofacial and vertebral/ocular abnormalities. Pierre Robin sequence has micrognathia with glossoptosis and often cleft palate, with airway/feeding implications. Distinguish these developmental syndromes from first-cleft fistulas through the parotid/ear region; they are not the same lesion category.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [Duke embryology: craniofacial development](https://embryology.oit.duke.edu/embryoModules/craniofacial/craniofacial.html)

docs.body:

For jejunoileal disease, inspect the full bowel for additional atresias, resect a short dysfunctional proximal segment when appropriate, preserve maximal length and create a well-perfused, tension-free anastomosis. Colonic atresia usually needs resection/anastomosis or staged diversion; consider distal aganglionosis before restoring continuity.

Distinguish it from IHPS; treatment may be membrane excision/pyloroplasty or gastroduodenostomy according to anatomy. Prognosis after any atresia depends on prematurity, associated abnormalities, sepsis, bowel length, dysmotility and intestinal-failure complications. Postoperative care includes gastric decompression, PN when required, gradual enteral feeds and growth monitoring.

### Necrotising enterocolitis

NEC results from interacting prematurity, intestinal barrier/immune immaturity, dysbiosis, feeding and perfusion injury. Excess inflammatory signalling, including TLR4-associated responses, cytokines and impaired repair contributes; it is not simply infection by one organism. Distinguish spontaneous intestinal perforation, which may present differently in extremely preterm infants.

Modified Bell staging: I suspected disease with feeding intolerance/distension and nonspecific systemic signs; II definite disease with characteristic intestinal findings such as pneumatosis (IIA) and more severe systemic/laboratory disease/portal gas or ascites (IIB); III advanced disease with severe instability, coagulopathy and peritonitis (IIIA without, IIIB with perforation). Radiographs may show pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, persistent dilated loops and free air. Ultrasound adds perfusion, wall thickness, portal gas and complex free fluid.

Stop feeds, decompress stomach, obtain cultures, start broad antimicrobial treatment according to local neonatal microbiology, support fluids/electrolytes/perfusion and respiratory function, and give PN when required. Serial examination, imaging, platelet count, lactate and acid-base trends matter more than one normal film. Free intraperitoneal air is a strong surgical indication; worsening clinical disease with suspected necrotic bowel, refractory shock, abdominal wall changes or deteriorating metabolic parameters may justify intervention without visible free air.

Laparotomy identifies necrosis, preserves viable bowel and provides resection with stoma or selected primary anastomosis. Peritoneal drainage is used in selected very small/unstable infants, with ongoing reassessment for definitive surgery; it is not necessarily curative. Pan-NEC involving nearly all bowel demands careful viability assessment, family discussion and bowel-preserving judgement; indiscriminate resection can create irreversible intestinal failure. Late problems include strictures (often colonic), short bowel, adhesions, cholestasis, growth and neurodevelopmental impairment. Persistent obstruction after recovery requires stricture evaluation.

### Cytokines and repair
Excess TNF-alpha, IL-1/IL-6-related inflammatory responses, endothelial injury and impaired epithelial repair can amplify NEC after microbial and perfusion insults in immature bowel. Growth/repair signals such as EGF influence mucosal resilience; breast-milk-associated protective factors and altered microbiota are part of the biological context. These mechanisms do not justify giving an unvalidated cytokine inhibitor or growth factor as routine neonatal therapy.

### Choledochal cyst and bilirubin metabolism

Bilirubin arises mainly from haem breakdown: haem oxygenase produces biliverdin, reduced to unconjugated bilirubin. Albumin carries it to the liver, UGT1A1 conjugates it, and canalicular transport excretes it into bile. Intestinal metabolism produces urobilinogen and faecal stercobilin; some undergoes enterohepatic circulation. Neonatal immaturity, haemolysis, breast-milk effects, hypothyroidism and conjugation disorders cause unconjugated jaundice; sepsis, BA, biliary cysts and hepatocellular/metabolic disease cause conjugated jaundice. Jaundice in the first day, rapid rise, prolonged jaundice, illness or conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia requires evaluation; pathological status is not defined by colour alone.

Todani types: I fusiform/cystic extrahepatic dilatation (subtypes Ia/Ib/Ic); II diverticulum; III choledochocele; IVa intra- and extrahepatic, IVb multiple extrahepatic; V Caroli disease. Draw normal ducts next to each schematic. Abnormal pancreaticobiliary junction and pancreatic reflux are important mechanisms, while developmental/obstructive factors also contribute. Forme-fruste disease has an abnormal junction and symptoms without striking duct dilatation.

Presentation includes neonatal cholestasis, pain, pancreatitis, cholangitis or a mass; the classic triad is uncommon. Ultrasound is initial imaging; MRCP defines biliary and pancreatic anatomy. Check liver tests, coagulation and pancreatic enzymes. In an infant, distinguish a cystic BA remnant from a communicating choledochal cyst before reconstruction.

For common extrahepatic types, complete cyst excision with cholecystectomy and a wide Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy is established treatment; hepaticoduodenostomy is an alternative with different reflux considerations. Carefully separate portal structures and define the distal intrapancreatic junction. Treat cholangitis/pancreatitis and correct vitamin-K-related coagulopathy before surgery where possible. Type II/III and intrahepatic disease need anatomy-specific treatment; diffuse Caroli disease with severe complications may require transplantation. Follow anastomotic stricture, stones, cholangitis, pancreatitis and residual malignancy risk; internal drainage without excision is not adequate definitive management for a usual type-I cyst.

![Original teaching schematic: todani. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/todani.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN infant cholestasis guideline](https://www.naspghan.org/files/documents/pdfs/position-papers/Guideline_for_the_Evaluation_of_Cholestatic.23.pdf)

docs.title: Omphalocele, gastroschisis, umbilical defects and complex associations
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Omphalocele, gastroschisis, umbilical defects and complex associations

Omphalocele is a midline defect at the umbilical ring with a membrane covering bowel and sometimes liver; the cord inserts into the sac. It reflects disturbed ventral-body-wall development/return of herniated viscera and has important chromosomal, cardiac and syndromic associations. Gastroschisis is usually right paraumbilical, without a sac and with a separate cord; vascular and body-fold hypotheses exist, and a single established mechanism should not be claimed. Exposed bowel may become oedematous and matted. Hernia of the cord is a smaller, generally bowel-containing defect at the cord base; avoid clamping through bowel.

Ultrasound defines sac, liver, bowel appearance, cord insertion, growth and associated defects; offer genetic assessment especially for omphalocele. Counsel about delivery at a surgical centre, neonatal stabilization, possible staged closure and prolonged feeding recovery. Caesarean birth is not required for every abdominal-wall defect; giant liver-containing defects require individual planning.

At birth protect bowel/sac with sterile nonadherent material and a transparent bag, prevent heat loss, decompress stomach, establish access and replace fluid losses with measured reassessment. Avoid twisting the bowel pedicle and prolonged transport pressure. Gastroschisis can have primary closure if reduction does not compromise ventilation/perfusion; a preformed silo permits gradual reduction when visceroabdominal disproportion exists. Sutureless closure can use the umbilical remnant with dressings; possible benefits include less anaesthesia, with later umbilical hernia a trade-off. Complex gastroschisis with atresia/ischaemia/perforation requires individualized bowel preservation and staged treatment.

Giant omphalocele, particularly with liver and pulmonary hypoplasia, may require staged closure or delayed nonoperative epithelialisation ('paint and wait') followed by later reconstruction. Select topical agents carefully because of systemic absorption/toxicity. Monitor ventilation, abdominal pressure, urine output, limb perfusion, infection, PN-associated liver disease and growth. Primary closure must not be forced if it produces compartment physiology.

Cantrell pentalogy consists of a supraumbilical abdominal defect, lower sternal defect, anterior diaphragmatic defect, diaphragmatic pericardial defect and intracardiac abnormality. OEIS is omphalocele, cloacal exstrophy, imperforate anus and spinal defects. Both require cardiac, urological, spinal and intestinal mapping and staged multidisciplinary repair; preserve bowel, bladder plate, genital tissue and continence potential. Beckwith-Wiedemann spectrum involves 11p15 imprinting abnormalities, with macroglossia, overgrowth, abdominal-wall defect, hypoglycaemia and embryonal-tumour risk; surveillance follows the genetic subtype and regional recommendations.

docs.title: Persistent cloaca, hydrocolpos and genital obstruction
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Persistent cloaca, hydrocolpos and genital obstruction

Persistent cloaca is convergence of rectum, vagina and urinary tract into one common channel. Classically a female has one perineal opening. Two openings require careful identification of urethra and vagina/rectal communication; do not label every absent-anus presentation as cloaca. Classification by common-channel length (approximately below or above 3 cm) is useful, but urethral length, vaginal anatomy, sacrum and function are essential to reconstruction planning. Posterior cloacal variants have a posteriorly placed common outlet.

The neonatal priorities are sepsis/obstruction control, reliable urinary drainage and drainage of hydrocolpos/hydrometrocolpos. A distended vagina can obstruct the ureters and compromise kidneys; it must be actively sought with pelvic ultrasound. Catheter drainage through the common channel may fail to decompress every vaginal compartment, requiring a dedicated catheter or vaginostomy. Create an appropriate colostomy where needed. Map renal anatomy and spinal/sacral/cardiac abnormalities.

Later evaluation uses examination under anaesthesia, cystoscopy/vaginoscopy, contrast cloacagram and pelvic MRI as needed. Identify common channel, urethral length to bladder neck, vagina(s), cervix/uterus, fistula and urinary drainage. A long common channel does not by itself determine the operation. Total urogenital mobilisation is suitable for selected anatomy; more complex cases require urogenital separation and sometimes vaginal replacement. Preserve blood supply, bladder neck and native urethra, and position the rectum within the sphincter complex. Genital repair needs future menstrual outflow and sexual function in mind.

MRKH syndrome is congenital absence/hypoplasia of the uterus and upper vagina in a person usually with 46,XX chromosomes and functioning ovaries. Associated renal/skeletal anomalies are important; vestibular fistula with vaginal agenesis requires recognition before rectal reconstruction. Other causes of hydrocolpos include imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum and distal vaginal atresia; treatment is anatomically specific. Counselling includes menstruation, fertility, body image and the potential need for later procedures. In cloaca, follow recurrent obstruction, renal function, continence, vaginal stenosis and pregnancy issues with a multidisciplinary team.

### Anorectal malformations, pouch colon and postoperative continence

### Classification and neonatal assessment
Use the Krickenbeck major groups: perineal fistula, rectourethral fistula (bulbar/prostatic), rectovesical fistula, vestibular fistula, cloaca, ARM without fistula and anal stenosis. Rare/regional variants include pouch colon, rectal atresia/stenosis, rectovaginal fistula and H-type fistula. Older 'high/intermediate/low' schemes are useful historically but do not replace fistula-based anatomy.

Inspect the perineum and count openings carefully. Look for meconium on skin, in urine or at the vestibule; a female with two vestibular openings can have vestibular/rectovaginal variants or an absent vagina, and is not automatically a persistent cloaca, which classically has one common opening. Examine sacrum, spine, cardiac, renal and limb systems (VACTERL). Ultrasound assesses kidneys/bladder, pelvic fluid and spine in early infancy; echocardiography and sacral imaging guide risk. A prone cross-table lateral radiograph after gas has reached the distal pouch helps estimate pouch-perineum distance in a newborn without a visible fistula; an early image can falsely imply a high pouch.

### Operative principles
A suitable perineal fistula may undergo primary anoplasty/limited PSARP in experienced hands. More complex or uncertain anatomy commonly requires a divided sigmoid colostomy, followed by a technically adequate distal colostogram under pressure and planned definitive repair. Preserve useful colon and ensure a noncommunicating distal limb. PSARP defines the fistula and positions bowel within the muscle complex; laparoscopic-assisted repair can help selected high rectourinary fistulas but does not suit every ARM. Protect the urethra, vagina, autonomic nerves and sphincters; avoid tension and narrow anoplasty.

Rectal atresia has a normal anus with an interruption more proximally; confirm extent and preserve the normal anal canal. An H-type fistula is an abnormal connection despite a patent normally situated anus, distinct from complete anorectal atresia. In pouch colon, a variable length of colon is replaced by a dilated pouch ending in a urinary/genital fistula. Types I-IV reflect increasing amounts of normal proximal colon; 'complete' commonly describes types I/II and 'incomplete' types III/IV. Treat neonatal obstruction/perforation, manage the fistula, preserve feasible colonic length and choose resection or pouch tubularisation with staged pull-through according to anatomy.

### Functional outcomes
Continence depends on sacral/spinal development, muscle quality and anatomical type, not only operative precision. Assess true incontinence versus overflow from megarectum/constipation. Review anatomy, radiographs and operative history; use a tailored bowel-management programme with laxatives for constipation, daily enemas or antegrade continence enemas when appropriate. Persistent leakage warrants assessment of misplaced anus, stricture or retained fistula; repeat surgery needs a correctable anatomical reason. Follow urinary function, sexuality, fertility, psychosocial health and transition care.

### Prognostic and reconstruction details
Sacral development, spinal cord abnormalities and quality of sphincter muscles contribute to future continence; classify bowel continence potential before counselling. Pouch-colon type I has no normal colon (ileum enters pouch), II has caecum proximal to pouch, III has a significant length of normal colon before pouch, and IV retains nearly normal colon with a distal pouch. Preserve useful normal bowel; tubularisation may be considered for selected extensive pouches, balancing motility and redilatation. A H-type perineal/rectourinary fistula with a normal anus must be separated from classic ARM before performing an unnecessary pull-through.

### Developmental basis
Early cloacal development integrates the terminal hindgut and allantoic/urogenital structures. During roughly weeks 4-7, differential growth and partitioning produce separate anorectal and urogenital outlets and the perineal region; abnormal development and fistulous connections produce the ARM spectrum. The older 'failure of urorectal septum descent' theory is a simplified account, not a complete explanation of every malformation. Genitourinary, sacral/spinal and vertebral abnormalities reflect the shared developmental field and should be actively assessed.

docs.title: Chest-wall deformities and pectus repair
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Chest-wall deformities and pectus repair

Examples include pectus excavatum, pectus carinatum, mixed/arcuatum deformity, Poland syndrome and sternal cleft. Assess cardiopulmonary symptoms, posture, scoliosis, connective-tissue syndromes and psychosocial impact. For excavatum, Haller index is transverse internal chest width divided by the minimum anteroposterior distance; a value near/above 3.25 is a commonly cited severity criterion, but symptoms, cardiac compression and functional tests matter. Correction index is another way to quantify depression and can be more informative in a nonstandard chest shape.

Evaluation includes examination, imaging sufficient for anatomy/severity, echocardiography for compression/associated cardiac abnormalities and selected pulmonary/exercise studies. Consider flexible bracing for carinatum and selected vacuum-bell treatment for suitable excavatum. Surgery is considered for significant physiological effects or severe deformity/psychosocial burden after informed discussion, not an index in isolation.

Nuss repair passes a contoured bar through the chest under thoracoscopic visualisation and rotates it to lift the sternum, then stabilises the bar. The crucial hazard is mediastinal/heart injury during tunnelling; visualisation, sternal elevation and a safe dissection path are essential. Analgesia, respiratory physiotherapy, bar-displacement prevention and planned removal form part of treatment. Modified Ravitch removes abnormal costal cartilage with preservation of perichondrium and corrects the sternum, useful in selected rigid/asymmetric anatomy. Complications include bleeding, pneumothorax, infection, bar displacement, recurrence and chronic pain.

Sternal clefts require assessment for cardiac/vascular and syndromic associations; early repair may be easier because of chest-wall flexibility. Cantrell defects require multidisciplinary sequencing, with protection of exposed heart/viscera and management of intracardiac disease. Do not equate every sternal cleft with complete Cantrell pentalogy.

### Quantifying severity and choosing correction
Measure Haller index at the plane of greatest depression; state the transverse width and minimal sternum-to-spine distance so the reader can reproduce it. Correction index expresses depression as (expected maximal AP distance minus the minimal AP distance) / expected maximal AP distance x 100%. Imaging methods and respiratory phase alter measurements. A narrow/deep or asymmetric chest can have misleading single-index classification; objective compression/exercise effects and patient symptoms add context.

For Nuss planning assess flexibility, asymmetry, prior operations and connective-tissue disease; choose bar number/shape and stabilization strategy. Place ports to visualize safe mediastinal passage, consider a sternal-elevation technique, tunnel under direct control and ensure no heart/pericardial injury. Bar rotation elevates the depression but can create pressure/displacement issues; explain restriction and follow-up until removal. In Ravitch-type surgery avoid excessive perichondrial destruction that may impair later chest growth. Bracing for flexible carinatum requires adherence and pressure monitoring; rigid/asymmetric or unsuccessful cases may need surgery.

An examination answer should specify why this child needs correction: physiological limitation, marked cardiac compression, significant severe deformity or well-assessed psychosocial burden after counselling. Routine CT in repeated surveillance may be unnecessary if lower-radiation assessment answers the question. For chest-wall variants, identify Poland's absence/hypoplasia of pectoral structures and possible hand anomalies, and distinguish mixed pectus arcuatum from isolated flexible carinatum.
