docs.title: Vascular tumours, malformations and Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Vascular tumours, malformations and Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon

Distinguish proliferative vascular tumours from structural vascular malformations. Infantile haemangiomas appear/grow after birth and then involute; congenital haemangiomas are fully formed at birth and have different involution patterns. Venous/lymphatic/capillary malformations are typically low flow; arteriovenous malformations have high-flow shunts. Name the classification version when asked: older simple/combined categories occur in past papers, while the current ISSVA structure emphasizes flow and biological grouping. Do not describe all vascular anomalies as 'haemangiomas'.

Assess depth, extent, flow, functional compromise and syndromic distribution with examination and Doppler; MRI maps deep lesions. Infantile haemangioma treatment is indicated for threatening airway/vision, ulceration, disfigurement risk or significant systemic effects. Propranolol acts through early vasoconstriction and longer effects on angiogenic signalling; assess cardiac/respiratory contraindications and educate about bradycardia, bronchospasm and hypoglycaemia, especially with fasting. Topical timolol suits selected small superficial lesions; corticosteroids/other systemic agents are selected alternatives. Laser and surgery have defined roles; they are not always first treatment for the proliferative phase.

Venous malformations may be managed with compression, image-guided sclerotherapy, selected excision and treatment of pain/thrombosis; extensive disease may need targeted systemic agents under a vascular-anomaly service. Lymphatic malformations respond to lesion-specific sclerotherapy/resection, with selected sirolimus or pathway-directed treatment for complex disease. CLOVES (congenital lipomatous overgrowth, vascular malformations, epidermal naevi, spinal/skeletal abnormalities) is within the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum.

Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon is severe thrombocytopenia/consumptive coagulopathy associated chiefly with kaposiform haemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma, not ordinary infantile haemangioma. Assess platelets, fibrinogen, coagulation and haemodynamic risk; management is urgent multidisciplinary tumour-directed therapy (commonly sirolimus-based/selected vincristine strategies), with blood products for bleeding/procedural need rather than automatic repeated platelet replacement. The historical term hepatic infantile haemangioendothelioma often refers to infantile hepatic haemangioma; distinguish focal congenital, multifocal and diffuse patterns, and assess high-output failure and consumptive hypothyroidism. Treat symptomatic disease and associated endocrine/cardiac consequences, with selected embolisation/surgery for refractory or anatomically appropriate lesions.

### Updated labels and drug mechanisms
The 2025 ISSVA classification also introduces potentially unique vascular anomaly (PUVA) terminology; use the full current schema for unusual lesions. Propranolol/timolol are beta blockers; systemic corticosteroids have anti-inflammatory/antiangiogenic effects and are alternatives in selected infantile-haemangioma cases. Historical interferon/vincristine treatments have toxicity limitations and are not routine first-line substitutes for propranolol. Sirolimus acts through mTOR and pathway-directed agents target selected molecular abnormalities in complex malformations; do not imply that every infantile haemangioma needs them.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [ISSVA Classification and Glossary (2025)](https://www.issva.org/classification)

docs.title: Hypospadias, curvature and graft urethroplasty
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Hypospadias, curvature and graft urethroplasty

Hypospadias combines a ventral ectopic meatus with variable curvature and deficient ventral foreskin; severity depends on curvature, plate/glans quality and penile dimensions as well as meatal site. Classify distal (glanular/coronal/distal shaft), midshaft and proximal (penoscrotal/scrotal/perineal). Disturbed androgen production/action and urethral-fold fusion contribute, with genetic/environmental factors. Preserve the prepuce until a reconstructive plan is made.

Proximal hypospadias with undescended testis, particularly bilateral nonpalpable testes, warrants DSD assessment: electrolytes, endocrine testing, karyotype/genetic evaluation and pelvic/gonadal anatomy under a multidisciplinary team. Routine renal imaging is not required in uncomplicated isolated distal hypospadias. Usual repair timing is infancy, commonly 6-18 months, individualized for health and resources. Goals are straight erection, a functional meatus, durable urethra and acceptable appearance.

At operation deglove and assess curvature with an erection test. Skin tethering may resolve after degloving; persistent curvature requires correction. Mild curvature can be corrected by dorsal plication with awareness of shortening; severe ventral curvature may need plate division and ventral corporotomy/lengthening, often with staged reconstruction. A good distal plate can undergo TIP/Snodgrass: incise the plate longitudinally, tubularise over a catheter and cover with a vascularised intermediate layer before glans closure. Onlay preputial island flap (Duckett onlay) augments a preserved plate; a tubularized island flap is a different operation. Severe proximal/poor-plate and redo cases may benefit from staged graft repair.

Buccal mucosa is useful in redo or deficient local tissue: defat the graft, secure on a vascular bed, allow maturation and then tubularise in a second stage when appropriate. It is a free graft and depends on plasmatic imbibition/revascularisation; an interposition dartos/tunica-vaginalis flap supplies vascular coverage and separates suture lines. Avoid taking scarred or diseased tissue. Preoperative androgen treatment is selective and evidence on benefit/complications is mixed; it is not compulsory.

Complications include fistula, meatal stenosis, urethral stricture, diverticulum, dehiscence, recurrent curvature and cosmetic/functional concerns. Assess stream and obstruction before repairing a fistula. Follow through puberty because late curvature and sexual-function issues may emerge. Balanitis xerotica obliterans/lichen sclerosus may affect foreskin, meatus and urethra; diagnosis is clinical with histology where indicated, treatment ranges from circumcision/topical therapy to specialist urethral reconstruction.

### Named distal repairs and onlay-flap steps
Selected glanular/coronal anatomy without meaningful curvature may suit MAGPI (meatal advancement and glanuloplasty); Mathieu uses a perimeatal flap, and a broad healthy plate can suit Thiersch-Duplay tubularisation. TIP expands options by incising the plate, while GAP (glans approximation) is selected for suitable deep-grooved glanular anatomy. Severe curvature or a poor plate changes the plan. For a Duckett onlay, harvest inner preputial tissue on its vascular pedicle, transfer without twisting, suture its margins as an onlay to the retained urethral plate and cover the reconstruction before glans/skin closure. Distinguish this from a tubularized flap and avoid using a damaged plate merely to preserve a one-stage plan.

![Original teaching schematic: hypospadias plan. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/hypospadias-plan.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU: Hypospadias](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology/chapter/hypospadias)

docs.title: Conjoined and heteropagus twins
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Conjoined and heteropagus twins

Conjoined twins are classified by fusion site: thoracopagus, omphalopagus, ischiopagus, pygopagus, craniopagus and other variants, with limb-number modifiers. Heteropagus has a dependent incompletely developed parasitic component attached to a more developed autosite. Define shared anatomy rather than infer separability solely from the external appearance.

Planning includes detailed cross-sectional imaging, echocardiography, angiography when needed, urinary/bowel and spinal mapping, organ-function assessment and shared-circulation evaluation. Thoracic cardiac sharing strongly affects prognosis. Ischiopagus can share pelvis, genital/urinary systems and distal bowel; ureteral drainage and continence reconstruction require precise mapping. Pygopagus may share sacrum, spinal cord, anorectal structures and urogenital outlets; MRI and contrast studies define the planes.

A multidisciplinary team rehearses separation, haemorrhage control, anaesthesia for each child, tissue coverage and postoperative needs. Tissue expanders can prepare skin cover in selected patients but risk infection, extrusion and pressure injury. Discuss staged versus single procedures, allocation of shared organs, likely function, ethical constraints and realistic family expectations. Emergency separation for a dying component differs from elective planning; decisions require individual anatomical and clinical judgement.

### Anatomy-driven investigations for pygopagus separation
Document whether the two children have separate spinal cords/dural sacs, a common spinal canal, shared sacrum and abnormal nerve roots. MRI with detailed sagittal/axial sequences is central; neurological examination and functional assessment identify baseline limitations. Map anal sphincters, distal recta, urinary tracts and external genitalia by clinical examination, ultrasound, cross-sectional imaging and selected contrast/endoscopic studies. Obtain vascular mapping where it changes a planned dissection, rather than assuming each child has an independent pelvic supply.

Evaluate cardiopulmonary and renal reserve, haemoglobin/coagulation and possible cross-circulation. Plan patient positioning, monitoring and lines so both anaesthesia teams retain access during separation. Surgical sequencing typically identifies safe neural and vascular planes before dividing bowel/urinary communications and allocating soft tissue for closure; exact order is anatomy specific. Coordinate neurosurgery, paediatric surgery, urology, orthopaedics and reconstruction. Postoperative risks include neurological loss, wound breakdown, CSF leak, continence problems and the need for staged rehabilitation.

For heteropagus examine feeding vessels and the parasitic component's attachments, including bowel/urinary connections; apparently nonfunctional tissue may share a critical vessel or organ segment with the autosite. Removal may be simpler than symmetric separation but is not always a superficial excision. Shared-organ allocation and potential survival/function for each child require explicit ethical and family discussion; a classification diagram alone cannot establish an operative plan.

docs.title: Neural-tube defects, tethered cord and the MOMS trial
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Neural-tube defects, tethered cord and the MOMS trial

Neural-tube defects include open myelomeningocele/myeloschisis and closed dysraphism such as lipomyelomeningocele, dermal sinus and split-cord malformation. Folate status, maternal diabetes, medications and genetic factors contribute. Prevention includes preconception folic acid and risk-specific higher-dose strategies through obstetric guidance. Ultrasound and maternal serum AFP support antenatal detection; detailed neurosonography/MRI assess associated CNS findings.

For open MMC, protect the lesion with sterile moist nonadherent material, position to avoid pressure, maintain warmth, assess neurological level, urinary function and hydrocephalus, and organise early neurosurgical closure after stabilization. Prevent infection and latex exposure. Follow hydrocephalus/Chiari II, lower-limb function, orthopaedic problems, renal/bladder function, bowel continence, skin pressure injuries and learning/psychosocial needs.

Tethered cord is pathological traction on the spinal cord, caused by lipoma, thick/tight filum, split-cord malformation, dermal sinus or postoperative scarring. Cutaneous signs, pain, progressive weakness, deformity or new bladder deterioration prompt MRI and neurological/urological assessment. Detethering is indicated for suitable progressive/symptomatic disease; prophylactic surgery in asymptomatic variants is individualized and controversial. Diastematomyelia/split cord has two hemicords separated by a bony/fibrous septum with one or two dural sacs; define the full anatomy before treatment.

Chiari I is predominantly tonsillar descent, Chiari II associates with MMC and hindbrain displacement, III involves hindbrain herniation into an encephalocele, and IV is a historical term for cerebellar hypoplasia. In symptomatic Chiari II first assess hydrocephalus/shunt function; selected persistent brainstem compression needs neurosurgical decompression.

The MOMS randomized trial compared prenatal and postnatal MMC repair in selected pregnancies. Prenatal repair reduced need for CSF shunting and improved some motor outcomes, with maternal uterine-scar and prematurity risks. It did not eliminate neurological/urological disability. Candidates require stringent maternal/fetal assessment and specialist facilities; discuss lifelong maternal obstetric consequences and possible repeat fetal/postnatal interventions. Outcomes from selected trial patients cannot be extrapolated to every fetus.

### CSF circulation, hydrocephalus and shunt complications

CSF is produced mainly by choroid plexus: lateral ventricles -> foramina of Monro -> third ventricle -> aqueduct -> fourth ventricle -> foramina of Magendie/Luschka -> cisterns/subarachnoid space -> venous and lymphatic clearance pathways. Hydrocephalus is disturbed CSF dynamics with ventricular enlargement; obstructive disease blocks an intraventricular pathway, whereas communicating disease often impairs downstream circulation/absorption. Causes include aqueduct stenosis, posterior-fossa lesions, haemorrhage, infection and congenital malformations.

Assess head growth/fontanelle in infants, vomiting/headache, papilloedema, developmental change and focal signs. Ultrasound through an open fontanelle, MRI and selected urgent CT demonstrate anatomy; ventricular size alone does not define clinical severity. VP shunting diverts CSF to the peritoneum. ETV creates an opening in the third-ventricle floor into the basal cisterns and is most suitable for selected obstructive disease; age, aetiology and prior shunt affect success. Choroid-plexus cauterisation is an additional selected strategy in some infant settings.

Early shunt problems include infection, blockage, malposition, haemorrhage and CSF leak; late problems include disconnection, migration, overdrainage, subdural collections, abdominal pseudocyst and bowel perforation. Suspected infection needs cultures and neurosurgical source-control/antimicrobial planning. Suspected malfunction is a clinical emergency; a small ventricle does not exclude failure. Slit-ventricle syndrome involves symptomatic shunted patients with small ventricles and abnormal pressure dynamics, potentially from overdrainage or intermittent obstruction. Management may require valve adjustment/antisiphon strategies or selected revision, guided by physiology.

Aqueductal stenosis may be treated by ETV or a shunt according to suitability. Prevent shunt complications through sterile technique, appropriate perioperative prophylaxis, sound catheter placement and structured surveillance. Families need clear warning symptoms and access to assessment. Agenesis of the corpus callosum is a developmental malformation with variable associated anomalies and developmental outcomes; investigate genetics/other CNS abnormalities and provide supportive neurodevelopmental care rather than treating it as an obstructive lesion automatically.

![Original teaching schematic: csf. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/csf.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [MOMS randomized trial: prenatal versus postnatal MMC repair](https://www.nejm.org/doi/abs/10.1056/nejmoa1014379)

docs.title: Bladder augmentation and continent urinary reconstruction
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Bladder augmentation and continent urinary reconstruction

Indications include refractory low capacity/poor compliance that threatens upper tracts or prevents acceptable continence despite catheterization, drugs and selected botulinum treatment; causes include neurogenic bladder and selected exstrophy/outlet reconstructions. Preoperative assessment documents urodynamics, renal function, bowel availability, nutritional status, infection, ability to catheterize and lifelong follow-up. Informed discussion must include dependence on CIC and risk of emergency perforation.

Detubularised ileum is commonly used because of availability and a compliant reservoir. Colon can provide a large patch but produces mucus and electrolyte exchange. Stomach has less mucus and may be considered in selected metabolic situations, but risks haematuria-dysuria syndrome, acid secretion, hypochloraemic alkalosis and ulceration; it is not the routine preferred segment. Ileum/colon can cause hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, particularly when renal function is poor. Ureterocystoplasty avoids intestinal metabolic consequences but requires a suitable dilated ureter and may provide limited capacity. Autoaugmentation has variable durability and smaller capacity gains.

Open the bladder widely, detubularise the bowel to prevent high-pressure peristaltic contractions, create a broad patch and obtain a watertight anastomosis with drainage. Preserve bowel and urinary blood supply. An appendicovesicostomy (Mitrofanoff) or reconfigured ileal Monti channel can allow catheterization through a continent abdominal stoma; it is a channel, not the reservoir itself. Select patients who can follow catheterization/irrigation reliably or have dependable assistance. Bladder-neck surgery must not create obstruction in an unsafe reservoir.

Early complications are leakage, ileus, bleeding, infection and bowel obstruction. Late complications include stones, mucus retention, symptomatic infection, metabolic acidosis, B12 deficiency after relevant ileal use, bowel symptoms, channel stenosis/leakage and spontaneous bladder perforation. Malignancy risk is a long-term consideration; investigation is symptom/risk guided rather than an assumed universal annual cystoscopy regimen. Acute abdominal pain in an augmented patient demands evaluation for perforation even with an initially nondiagnostic scan. Follow reservoir pressures, residuals, renal function, electrolytes, ultrasound and catheterization adherence through transition to adult services.

### Alternatives and postoperative safeguards
The common bowel-based choices are ileocystoplasty, colocystoplasty and selected gastrocystoplasty; less common approaches include ureterocystoplasty and autoaugmentation. Detubularisation reduces coordinated bowel contractions and increases reservoir compliance. Gastrocystoplasty can be less favourable because of painful acid secretion/haematuria-dysuria and alkalosis; do not describe its lower mucus production as absence of serious long-term risk. After augmentation ensure adequate catheter drainage, mucus irrigation when prescribed, and an emergency plan for pain/distension or inability to catheterize.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

docs.title: VUR, UTIs and ureteric reimplantation
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### VUR, UTIs and ureteric reimplantation

Primary VUR is failure of the ureterovesical antireflux mechanism, often due to a short intramural tunnel. Secondary VUR results from raised bladder pressure or outlet dysfunction. Grade I reflux reaches ureter only; II reaches collecting system without dilatation; III has mild/moderate dilatation; IV has moderate dilatation/tortuosity with blunted fornices; V has gross dilatation/tortuosity and loss of papillary impressions. Reflux nephropathy includes congenital dysplasia and acquired scarring after febrile pyelonephritis; reflux does not by itself explain every scar.

Risk factors for childhood UTI include VUR/obstruction, bladder-bowel dysfunction, incomplete emptying, instrumentation and selected congenital anomalies. Obtain a reliable urine specimen and culture before treatment where practical. Ultrasound identifies anatomy; VCUG defines reflux and urethra; DMSA assesses cortical defects/scarring. A top-down strategy starts with renal parenchymal assessment in selected febrile UTI cases and uses VCUG selectively, rather than studying reflux first in everyone. Imaging strategies vary with age and guideline; radiation and whether results change management matter.

Treat infection promptly and manage constipation/voiding dysfunction. Observation with or without prophylaxis is selected according to grade, age, renal abnormalities and febrile-UTI risk. Surgery is considered for breakthrough febrile UTI despite appropriate treatment, persistent high-risk reflux/renal deterioration, poor feasibility of surveillance/prophylaxis, or associated anatomical indications. Correct unsafe bladder pressures first.

Endoscopic injection creates a supportive mound beneath the intramural ureter. STING places the needle subureterically; HIT uses hydrodistention and injection within the ureteral tunnel, with double-HIT variants. Advantages are short intervention and low morbidity; success is lower in higher grades/complex anatomy and reinjection or reimplantation may be needed. Risks include obstruction, persistence and recurrent reflux.

Open reimplantation options include intravesical Cohen cross-trigonal, Politano-Leadbetter and Glenn-Anderson advancement, and extravesical Lich-Gregoir. A tunnel-length/ureter-diameter ratio around 5:1 (Paquin principle) is a useful surgical concept, while blood supply and tension-free alignment remain crucial. Vesicoscopic Cohen uses intravesical ports/pneumovesicum; robotic reimplantation commonly uses an extravesical approach. Mobilise without devascularizing, preserve nerves, construct the tunnel and confirm unobstructed drainage. Bilateral extravesical dissection risks transient retention. Complications include obstruction, persistent reflux, urine leak and voiding dysfunction.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

docs.title: Testicular descent, impalpable testis and orchidopexy
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Testicular descent, impalpable testis and orchidopexy

Testicular descent has a transabdominal phase influenced by INSL3/gubernacular development and regression of the cranial suspensory ligament, followed by an androgen/genitofemoral-nerve/CGRP-associated inguinoscrotal phase in later gestation. Distinguish undescended, ectopic, retractile, ascending and absent/vanishing testes. Ectopic sites include superficial inguinal pouch, perineum, femoral region and transverse scrotal ectopia.

Examine warm, relaxed children and document testis size/site, scrotum and associated hernia/hypospadias. Routine ultrasound for a nonpalpable testis often fails to locate it and should not postpone specialist assessment. Bilateral nonpalpable testes require prompt endocrine/DSD evaluation, particularly if genital ambiguity or hypoglycaemia/electrolyte abnormalities coexist. AMH/inhibin B and selected hormone tests assess testicular tissue/function; imaging cannot conclusively prove anorchia.

Persistent congenital undescended testis after 6 months corrected age usually needs orchidopexy, completed preferably by 12 months and at latest around 18 months. Hormonal treatment is not a reliable alternative to surgery for inducing descent; fertility-directed hormonal strategies are specialist and not universally adopted. Palpable testes undergo mobilisation, hernia-sac management and tension-free fixation in a subdartos pouch, preserving vas and vessels. Diagnostic laparoscopy for impalpable testes distinguishes intra-abdominal testis, blind-ending vessels and vessels entering the ring, directing further exploration.

A high intra-abdominal testis with insufficient vessel length may need staged Fowler-Stephens orchidopexy: divide testicular vessels and rely on vasal/cremasteric collateral supply, preserving the collateral arcade. A staged approach allows collateral development; traction techniques are alternatives in selected centres. Risks include atrophy, re-ascent, vas injury and hernia. Cryptorchidism increases subfertility, torsion and malignancy risk; early orchidopexy improves surveillance and fertility potential but does not abolish cancer risk.

### Fowler-Stephens selection and follow-up
Before sacrificing testicular vessels, determine whether further mobilisation or a different tension-reducing strategy can achieve safe descent. A low intra-abdominal testis may descend on intact vessels; a high testis more often needs staged collateral-based surgery. Preserve the vasal vascular arcade and avoid collateral injury during later mobilisation. Assess postoperative position and volume; inform families about atrophy, re-ascent and the need for later examination. Retractile testes generally need surveillance for ascent rather than immediate orchidopexy.

### Timeline and signalling
The transabdominal phase is mainly around weeks 8-15; the inguinoscrotal phase is predominantly around weeks 25-35, with variation. INSL3/RXFP2 signalling and gubernacular enlargement are central to the first phase; androgen action, genitofemoral-nerve signalling and gubernacular migration are important later. Testicular descent is a coordinated developmental process, not simply pressure pushing a testis down a canal.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

docs.title: Intestinal failure, nutrition and transplantation
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Intestinal failure, nutrition and transplantation

Short-bowel syndrome is malabsorption after loss of functional small intestine; intestinal failure is inability to maintain adequate nutrition/hydration without parenteral support. Residual length must be interpreted with gestational age, bowel segment, colon continuity, ileocaecal valve and adaptation; a universal length cutoff is misleading. Causes include NEC, volvulus, atresia and gastroschisis. Loss of ileum affects bile-acid/B12 absorption; colon can salvage fluid and carbohydrate energy.

Early care replaces measured fluid/electrolyte losses, gives individualized PN and introduces enteral nutrition as tolerated to stimulate adaptation. Protect central access, avoid overfeeding and monitor triglycerides, glucose, micronutrients and liver function. Treat bacterial overgrowth and specific malabsorption; use acid suppression in selected early hypersecretory states and antimotility treatment when appropriate. Intestinal rehabilitation coordinates surgery, gastroenterology, nutrition and nursing. GLP-2 analogues are selected specialist therapy subject to age/approval and careful monitoring.

Surgery first corrects obstruction, restores continuity and preserves bowel. STEP and longitudinal intestinal lengthening/tailoring (Bianchi) may improve a suitably dilated bowel with persistent dysfunction; neither creates new mucosal mass, and both risk leak, ischaemia and recurrent dilatation. Assess length, vascular pattern, diameter and liver disease before selecting an operation.

Transplant consideration is driven by failure/serious complications of rehabilitation and PN, including progressive intestinal-failure-associated liver disease, threatened loss of central access and recurrent life-threatening catheter sepsis. Assess anatomy, liver/renal function, thrombosis, infections, nutritional status, cardiopulmonary fitness, psychosocial support and immunology. Types include isolated intestine, combined liver-intestine and multivisceral grafts, with modified multivisceral variants. Implant vascular inflow/outflow and intestinal continuity, often with a monitoring access/stoma; immunosuppression and repeated rejection surveillance are essential. Rejection, infection, graft-versus-host disease, PTLD and vascular complications affect outcomes. Long-term PN dependence alone is not an automatic transplant indication.

docs.title: Alimentary duplications, Meckel diverticulum and mesenteric lesions
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Alimentary duplications, Meckel diverticulum and mesenteric lesions

Enteric duplications characteristically have alimentary epithelial lining, a smooth-muscle wall and close association/shared blood supply with native bowel. Cystic and tubular forms can occur anywhere; multiple developmental theories include abnormal recanalisation, split notochord and embryonic diverticula, none explaining every case. Ectopic gastric mucosa can bleed or ulcerate. Presentation includes prenatal/neonatal mass, obstruction, pain, bleeding, intussusception or infection. Ultrasound may show a double-wall/gut-signature sign; MRI/contrast studies map complex thoracic or pelvic lesions.

Resect the duplication with adjacent bowel when shared blood supply requires it; preserve length, especially for long tubular lesions, where mucosal stripping or tailored surgery may be considered. Rectal/colonic duplications need pelvic/urinary mapping; avoid sphincter, nerve and ureter injury. A cystic lymphatic malformation in the mesentery differs histologically from an enteric duplication; resection or selected sclerotherapy depends on relation to bowel vessels and symptoms.

Meckel diverticulum is a vitelline/omphalomesenteric-duct remnant on the antimesenteric ileal border. Remnants include patent duct, sinus, cyst, fibrous band and diverticulum. Complications include bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa, inflammation, obstruction/bands, volvulus and intussusception. A 99mTc-pertechnetate scan detects functioning gastric mucosa rather than the diverticulum itself; fasting/appropriate preparation and selected acid-suppression protocols improve technique, but false results occur. Treat symptomatic disease with diverticulectomy or segmental ileal resection depending on base, inflammation and location of ectopic tissue.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11) combines mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous polyps with obstruction/intussusception and cancer risk; surveillance and polyp clearance aim to preserve bowel. Familial adenomatous polyposis (APC) produces numerous adenomas and high colorectal-cancer risk; genetic counselling, lower/upper-GI surveillance and prophylactic colorectal surgery are individualized to polyp burden and extracolonic disease.

docs.title: Neonatal cholestasis, biliary atresia and Kasai outcomes
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Neonatal cholestasis, biliary atresia and Kasai outcomes

### Recognition and investigation
Conjugated jaundice is pathological. Persistent jaundice, pale/acholic stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly warrant prompt direct bilirubin measurement and hepatobiliary assessment. A direct bilirubin above 1 mg/dL is an important abnormal threshold; the older requirement that it exceed 20% of total bilirubin can miss disease. Differential diagnosis includes biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, infection, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Alagille syndrome, metabolic/endocrine disorders, genetic bile-transport disease and parenteral-nutrition-associated cholestasis.

Assess stool colour, growth, bleeding and splenic/associated abnormalities. Tests include fractionated bilirubin, liver enzymes/GGT, albumin, glucose, INR (including response to vitamin K), CBC, cultures when needed and targeted metabolic/genetic investigations. Fasting ultrasound assesses gallbladder morphology, triangular-cord sign, ducts, cysts and vascular anatomy. No single negative ultrasound or scintigraphic result reliably excludes BA. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy can demonstrate excretion; absent excretion is nonspecific and must not delay definitive evaluation. Liver biopsy often shows bile duct proliferation, bile plugs, portal oedema and fibrosis. Intraoperative cholangiography establishes extrahepatic patency/anatomy when BA is suspected.

### Pathology and operation
BA is progressive fibro-obliterative cholangiopathy with interacting developmental, inflammatory and immune mechanisms. CMV-associated BA is a described subgroup; association does not prove CMV causes all BA, and antiviral treatment needs specialist selection. Anatomical types are I (common bile duct), II (common hepatic duct, with subtypes), and III (at porta hepatis; most common). A cystic hilar lesion may represent cystic BA rather than a patent choledochal cyst; assess distal patency and hepatic ducts.

Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy removes the fibrotic extrahepatic remnant and exposes microscopic ductules at the portal plate, connected to a Roux-en-Y jejunal limb. Earlier diagnosis and surgery improve the chance of bile drainage; age is not the sole criterion. Avoid damage to portal vessels and inappropriate deep excision. Provide high-energy nutrition, fat-soluble vitamins, cholangitis treatment and surveillance. The benefit of routine steroids is unsettled and protocol dependent.

### Prognosis and transplantation
Jaundice clearance and bilirubin after Kasai, age/fibrosis at operation, anatomical/syndromic disease, recurrent cholangitis, centre experience and portal hypertension influence native-liver survival. Some children retain native liver long term, while others develop cirrhosis despite initial bile drainage. Follow growth, fat-soluble vitamins, coagulopathy, varices, ascites, hepatopulmonary syndrome and malignancy surveillance where indicated. Refer early for transplant assessment after failed drainage, progressive decompensation, refractory portal-hypertension complications, severe growth failure or recurrent uncontrollable cholangitis. Kasai is a bridge to long-term native-liver health or transplantation, rather than a guaranteed cure.

### Paediatric kidney/liver transplantation and immunosuppression

Kidney-transplant candidates have irreversible kidney failure and acceptable overall fitness; select pre-emptive transplantation where feasible. Evaluate cause of failure/recurrence risk, urine drainage and bladder pressures, infection, vaccines, cardiovascular/nutritional status, vascular anatomy, sensitisation/HLA compatibility and adherence/support. A hostile bladder must be made safe before or with transplantation. Living-related/unrelated and deceased-donor grafts have different logistical/ischaemic considerations; small recipients require careful vascular planning, perfusion and fluid management.

Liver indications include decompensated chronic disease, BA with failed native-liver course, acute liver failure, selected metabolic conditions and selected unresectable tumours. Grafts can be whole deceased-donor, reduced/split or living-donor segmental grafts. The left lateral segments II/III are common for smaller children; a full left lobe includes IV. Assess graft-to-recipient size, vascular/biliary variants and donor safety. Living-donor procurement requires anatomical imaging, mobilization, identification of inflow/outflow and duct, parenchymal transection with adequate donor remnant, and controlled division/reconstruction. Split liver usually produces a left lateral graft for a child and a right-sided graft for another recipient; precise variant and vascular division planning matter.

Small-child challenges include size mismatch, hepatic-artery/portal thrombosis, limited abdominal capacity and variable venous drainage. Use meticulous microsurgical vascular technique, appropriate graft selection and surveillance Doppler. Postoperative care balances perfusion and fluid overload, immunosuppression, infection control, nutrition and rejection assessment. Complications include vascular thrombosis, bile leak/stricture, rejection, infection and PTLD. Prognosis depends on indication, recipient/graft factors and centre practice; avoid an unqualified universal survival percentage.

Immunosuppressants: calcineurin inhibitors tacrolimus/ciclosporin block T-cell activation (nephrotoxicity, hypertension and metabolic/neurotoxicity); steroids have broad anti-inflammatory effects (growth/metabolic/infection risks); mycophenolate inhibits purine synthesis (marrow/GI toxicity, teratogenicity); azathioprine is a purine antimetabolite (marrow/hepatic toxicity); mTOR inhibitors inhibit proliferation (wound, lipid and marrow effects). Induction may use anti-IL2-receptor or lymphocyte-depleting agents. Drug choice/levels are organ- and protocol-specific. Surveillance includes trough levels, organ function, viral disease, malignancy risk and lifelong adherence/transition support.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN infant cholestasis guideline](https://www.naspghan.org/files/documents/pdfs/position-papers/Guideline_for_the_Evaluation_of_Cholestatic.23.pdf)
- [NIDDK: Kidney transplantation](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/kidney-failure/kidney-transplant)
- [NCI PDQ: Childhood liver cancer, professional version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/liver/hp/child-liver-treatment-pdq?cid=eb_govdel_esp)

docs.title: Intestinal rotation, malrotation and midgut volvulus
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Intestinal rotation, malrotation and midgut volvulus

The midgut elongates, herniates physiologically into the umbilical cord around week 6 and rotates approximately 270 degrees counterclockwise around the SMA, viewed from the front, during herniation and return around week 10. Subsequent fixation places the duodenojejunal junction left of the spine and the caecum in the right lower quadrant, producing a broad mesenteric base. Nonrotation, incomplete rotation and abnormal fixation leave a narrow base and obstructing peritoneal bands; reversed rotation and internal hernia variants occur.

Bilious vomiting in a neonate demands urgent exclusion of volvulus. Older children may have intermittent pain/vomiting, poor growth or acute ischaemia. Stable patients usually undergo an upper-GI contrast study to locate the duodenojejunal junction and identify a corkscrew appearance. Ultrasound may show abnormal SMA/SMV relation and a whirlpool of mesentery/SMV around the SMA; vessel inversion alone is not definitive. In shock, peritonitis or strong evidence of ischaemic volvulus, resuscitation and surgery must not be delayed for a complete imaging sequence.

Keep nil by mouth; decompress stomach, obtain IV/IO access, restore perfusion, administer antibiotics for suspected ischaemia, and monitor lactate/electrolytes. At operation inspect viability, detorse the usual clockwise volvulus counterclockwise, divide Ladd bands, mobilise the duodenum/right colon and broaden the mesenteric base. Place small bowel predominantly on the right and colon on the left; appendicectomy is commonly performed because the caecum remains ectopic. The Ladd procedure does not restore normal embryological rotation. Reassess questionable bowel after reperfusion; preserve length and consider a planned second look rather than aggressive removal of potentially recoverable intestine.

Laparoscopy is feasible for stable selected cases, but gross distension, suspected ischaemia or instability may favour open surgery. Ensure mesenteric broadening is adequate. Long-term problems include adhesive obstruction, rare recurrent volvulus, persistent symptoms and short bowel after extensive resection. Families should seek immediate assessment for recurrent bilious vomiting.

![Original teaching schematic: malrotation. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/malrotation.svg)

docs.title: Empyema, chylothorax, mediastinal masses and lung hydatid
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Empyema, chylothorax, mediastinal masses and lung hydatid

Empyema evolves from exudative fluid to fibrinopurulent loculation and organising peel. Treat underlying infection, obtain cultures where practical, use ultrasound to map fluid and provide antibiotics. Significant complicated fluid needs drainage; intrapleural fibrinolysis and VATS are accepted approaches according to disease stage/resources, while routine open decortication for every effusion is unnecessary. VATS drains pus, breaks loculations and removes restrictive material while preserving lung. Streptokinase is historical/one option; agent choice follows the paediatric service protocol. Complications include bleeding, air leak, bronchopleural fistula and incomplete drainage. Empyema necessitans extends through the chest wall; evaluate organisms including TB where appropriate and drain/treat the intrathoracic source.

Chylothorax is leakage of lymph from the thoracic duct/tributaries, congenital or after injury/surgery. Fluid triglycerides and chylomicrons support diagnosis; fasting fluid need not be milky. Drain respiratory-compromising effusion and monitor protein, electrolytes, lymphocyte and fat-soluble nutrient loss. Reduce chyle flow with an MCT-based feeding plan or PN when needed; selected octreotide and lymphatic imaging/intervention are options. Persistent high-output leakage may need embolisation or operative ligation. Avoid prolonged uncontrolled nutritional and immune depletion.

Classify mediastinal lesions by anterior/prevascular (thymic, lymphoma, germ-cell), middle/visceral (bronchogenic/duplication cysts, nodes) and posterior/paravertebral (neurogenic tumours, meningoceles). An anterior mass can cause catastrophic airway/vascular collapse with sedation: assess symptoms, compression and positional tolerance before biopsy/anaesthesia. Posterior masses require MRI for intraspinal extension, tumour markers as indicated and safe tissue diagnosis; treat neuroblastoma according to risk rather than reflex immediate total excision.

Lung hydatid can present with cough, chest pain, haemoptysis, infection or cyst rupture. Imaging defines intact/ruptured cysts and other organ disease. Avoid percutaneous puncture of a lung cyst without a specialised plan. Treatment often uses parenchyma-preserving cyst removal with prevention of spillage and bronchial-leak closure, with antiparasitic therapy selected by an experienced team. Flail chest (segment of ribs moving independently) causes pain and ventilatory impairment; treat analgesia, oxygenation and associated lung injury, with drainage of pneumothorax/haemothorax when indicated. Positive-pressure ventilation is driven by respiratory failure, not rib pattern alone.

### Cystic lesions and chest-wall extension
Mediastinal cysts include bronchogenic, oesophageal duplication, thymic, pericardial and lymphatic lesions; selected posterior neurenteric/meningeal lesions require spinal mapping. Resection/observation depends on symptoms, compression, diagnostic certainty and operative risk. In empyema necessitans, define both intrathoracic infection and the chest-wall tract/collection; draining the external lump alone can leave an ongoing infected pleural source. Obtain microbiology including TB evaluation where appropriate and restore pleural drainage/lung expansion. In flail chest, pulmonary contusion and pain often explain respiratory failure; physiotherapy, analgesia and respiratory support are individualized, with chest drainage for associated pleural injury and selected fixation rather than automatic intubation solely because ribs are fractured.

docs.title: Oesophageal atresia, long-gap reconstruction and substitution
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Oesophageal atresia, long-gap reconstruction and substitution

Gross types are A (atresia without fistula), B (proximal fistula), C (distal fistula; commonest), D (proximal and distal fistulae) and E (H-type fistula without atresia). Disturbed foregut dorsoventral patterning/separation involving pathways such as SHH contributes; a literal failed septum is an oversimplification. Associations include VACTERL (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal and limb), VACTERL-H (hydrocephalus) and CHARGE (coloboma, heart disease, choanal atresia, growth/developmental problems, genital and ear abnormalities).

Drooling/choking, inability to pass an orogastric tube and a coiled tube on radiograph suggest EA. Abdominal gas implies a distal fistula; a gasless abdomen suggests pure atresia but is not absolute. Protect airway, elevate head, continuously suction the upper pouch with a Replogle tube, avoid feeding and assess cardiac/renal/vertebral anatomy. Bronchoscopy locates fistulae and airway abnormalities when feasible. Prognostic schemes include Waterston (birth weight, pneumonia, anomalies) and Spitz (birth weight below 1.5 kg and major cardiac disease); contemporary outcomes also depend on prematurity and pulmonary status.

Primary repair separates/ligates the fistula and creates a well-perfused tension-conscious oesophageal anastomosis. Thoracoscopy offers improved visualisation and cosmesis in selected stable infants, but requires expertise and vigilance for hypercapnia, acidosis and tension. Open repair remains appropriate for unstable or complex patients. Most contained anastomotic leaks can be managed with drainage, nutritional support, antibiotics as indicated and time; major uncontrolled leaks need individualized revision. Later stricture is treated by controlled endoscopic dilatation; assess reflux and eosinophilic inflammation, with adjuncts/reoperation reserved for refractory cases.

Long-gap EA is defined functionally by inability to obtain a safe primary anastomosis, rather than a universal centimetre cut-off. Preserve native oesophagus when feasible: gastrostomy/nutrition and upper-pouch drainage followed by delayed primary anastomosis, or specialist traction/lengthening approaches. Foker traction may stimulate growth but needs repeated procedures and carries leak, reflux, stricture and intensive-care burdens. Magnamosis uses magnetic compression to join suitable closely apposed pouches; it remains a selected evolving technique, with stricture/reintervention concerns.

Replacement options include gastric pull-up (right gastroepiploic/right gastric supply), gastric tube (usually right gastroepiploic based), colon (selected colic pedicle assessed for continuity) and jejunum (mesenteric arcades, sometimes microvascular augmentation). Routes are posterior mediastinal, retrosternal or selected subcutaneous; posterior is shortest but prior mediastinal scarring/fistula may make alternatives preferable. Ensure vascularity, length without redundancy, tension-free anastomoses and no torsion. Gastric pull-up can cause respiratory compromise, leak, delayed emptying, reflux/dumping and intrathoracic distension; colon can develop redundancy and anastomotic problems; jejunum is peristaltic but technically demanding. Tissue-engineered oesophageal replacements are investigational. Lifelong review addresses swallowing, strictures, reflux, tracheomalacia, recurrent fistula and nutrition.

### H-type fistula and associated anomalies
An H-type fistula can present with coughing/cyanosis during feeds and recurrent respiratory infection despite a patent oesophagus. Contrast studies may miss it; targeted contrast technique and bronchoscopy help locate the tract. Plan cervical versus thoracic exposure by fistula level, divide the connection and close tracheal/oesophageal defects separately with protection of recurrent laryngeal nerves. Evaluate recurrence and airway dysfunction. For long-gap replacement, identify both the conduit blood supply and the route: an excellent conduit can fail from tension, pedicle twisting or a poorly chosen mediastinal passage.

### Spitz groups for the classification subpart
Group I has birth weight at least 1500 g and no major cardiac disease; group II has either weight below 1500 g or major cardiac disease; group III has both factors. These are historical prognostic groups, not indications to withhold repair. Waterston's earlier scheme used weight plus pneumonia/associated abnormalities. Do not attach a historical survival percentage to a contemporary centre without specifying the study era and population.

### Minimally invasive surgery, robotics, tissue engineering and gene/cell therapy

Paediatric MIS includes selected thoracic, abdominal and urological procedures: EA/lung surgery, diaphragmatic repair, appendicectomy, pyloromyotomy, fundoplication, pyeloplasty and selected tumour operations. Physiological tolerance, working space, lesion anatomy and surgeon experience govern suitability. Consider CO2-related hypercapnia/acidosis, pressure effects, hypothermia and trocar injury in small infants. Better cosmesis and smaller wounds do not justify an incomplete or unsafe operation.

Robotic systems include console-controlled telemanipulation and other task-specific platforms; most contemporary systems assist the surgeon rather than operate autonomously. Benefits include magnified 3-D vision, articulated instruments and tremor filtering; limitations include instrument size/spacing, cost, setup time, limited tactile feedback and small-patient constraints. Docking positions and connects robotic arms after safe port placement, avoiding collisions and ensuring emergency access. A robotic extravesical reimplantation needs ureteral mobilisation, detrusor tunnel creation and closure with preservation of perfusion and pelvic nerves. Single-incision, mini-instrument and selected natural-orifice approaches can improve cosmesis but have ergonomic/technical trade-offs. Training uses simulation, supervised modular progression, objective skills assessment and outcome review.

Tissue engineering combines cells, scaffold and biological/mechanical signals to form useful tissue. Potential paediatric applications include intestine, oesophagus, bladder and airway reconstruction, but achieving vascularisation, innervation, mechanical durability, barrier function and growth with the child is difficult. Biocompatibility, infection, fibrosis, GMP manufacture and long-term tumour safety limit translation. Do not describe an experimental engineered organ as established clinical replacement.

Stem cells have self-renewal and differentiation capacity; embryonic, induced pluripotent and tissue-specific sources differ in potency/ethical/safety issues. Mesenchymal stromal cells have immunomodulatory/paracrine properties, but should not automatically be claimed to regenerate every organ. Possible research applications include intestinal injury, neural defects, tissue scaffolds and wound healing. Gene therapy uses vectors/editing to modify cellular gene function; vector delivery, off-target effects, immune responses and durable expression require disease-specific evidence. Nanotechnology includes drug-delivery systems, imaging probes and biosensors, with biodistribution/toxicity issues. 3-D printing converts segmented imaging into models or guides useful for anatomy, operative planning, education and selected implants; print accuracy depends on segmentation and validation.

![Original teaching schematic: ea types. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/ea-types.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [ERNICA long-gap EA consensus (original publication)](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10098498/)
- [ERNICA guidelines and endorsed statements](https://www.ern-ernica.eu/guidelines)
- [Spitz: Oesophageal atresia at-risk groups (1994)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8078005/)

docs.title: Hirschsprung disease: diagnosis, pull-through and postoperative obstruction
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Hirschsprung disease: diagnosis, pull-through and postoperative obstruction

### Pathogenesis, genetics and diagnosis
Failure of neural-crest-derived enteric cells to populate distal bowel produces contiguous distal aganglionosis of submucosal and myenteric plexuses. The affected segment fails to relax, with proximal dilatation. RET-pathway abnormalities are central; EDNRB, EDN3, SOX10 and other genes contribute. Associations include Down syndrome, Waardenburg-Shah syndrome and Mowat-Wilson syndrome. Genetic counselling is especially relevant in familial, syndromic and long-segment disease.

Presentations include delayed meconium, neonatal obstruction, enterocolitis, failure to thrive or childhood constipation. Rectal examination may produce explosive stool but is neither necessary nor confirmatory. Contrast enema can show a transition zone, reversed rectosigmoid ratio and delayed evacuation; it may be misleading in neonates and total colonic disease. Anorectal manometry demonstrates an absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR), but histology establishes the diagnosis.

Take adequate rectal suction biopsies above the physiologically hypoganglionic anal zone, with sufficient submucosa; a full-thickness biopsy is used when suction tissue is inadequate or results conflict. H&E assesses absent ganglion cells and hypertrophic nerves. Increased acetylcholinesterase activity supports diagnosis; absent mucosal/submucosal calretinin staining is useful. Interpret with specimen quality, age and expert pathology. Intraoperative biopsies must demonstrate ganglionated bowel clear of the transition zone.

### Definitive operation
Decompress with rectal irrigations, correct sepsis/nutrition and map the disease. Selected stable, decompressed rectosigmoid cases can have a single-stage transanal endorectal pull-through; diversion is appropriate for instability, severe enterocolitis, difficult decompression or extensive disease. Swenson removes the aganglionic rectum with a low anastomosis; Soave pulls ganglionated bowel through an endorectal muscular cuff; Duhamel creates a retrorectal pull-through and joins it to the retained anterior rectum. Preserve sphincters and dentate-line sensation; avoid twist, tension, ischaemia and a restrictive cuff.

Total colonic aganglionosis requires serial biopsies including small bowel; imaging alone cannot define its proximal extent. Emergency diversion must be placed in proven ganglionated bowel. Definitive ileoanal pull-through options include straight/Soave-type or modified Duhamel reconstruction, chosen with nutritional and continence implications. Follow hydration, growth, sodium loss, skin injury and enterocolitis. “Ultra-short segment” disease is controversial: distinguish internal anal sphincter achalasia (absent RAIR with ganglion cells) and functional constipation before proposing resection.

### Persistent symptoms after surgery
First distinguish true incontinence from overflow due to obstruction. Obtain operative/histology records, examination under anaesthesia, contrast enema, and repeat biopsy when indicated. Mechanical causes include stricture, twisted pull-through, retained Soave cuff or Duhamel spur; histological causes include transition-zone pull-through/residual aganglionosis. Functional causes include internal sphincter achalasia and dysmotility. Treat demonstrable structural disease appropriately; use irrigations, a structured bowel regimen and selected botulinum toxin injection for outlet dysfunction. Redo surgery needs a defined cause and experienced team. Long-term surveillance covers continence, constipation, HAEC, psychosocial health and transition to adult care.

![Original teaching schematic: pullthrough. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/pullthrough.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [ERNICA rectosigmoid Hirschsprung guideline (2020)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7318734/)

docs.title: Caustic ingestion, stricture and endoscopy
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Caustic ingestion, stricture and endoscopy

Acids often cause coagulative necrosis and may injure the stomach prominently; alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis and can penetrate deeply into the oesophageal wall. Actual injury depends on concentration, amount, contact time and formulation, so these are tendencies rather than reliable predictions. Toilet-cleaner ingestion requires immediate airway and poisoning assessment, history of agent/amount/time and examination for pain, drooling, vomiting, stridor, chest/abdominal tenderness or shock. Oral burns do not reliably predict oesophageal injury.

Do not induce vomiting or attempt acid-alkali neutralisation; avoid blind gastric instrumentation and routine activated charcoal for corrosives. Keep symptomatic patients nil by mouth, protect airway when required and obtain IV support. Seek toxicology and paediatric gastroenterology/surgical input. Chest/abdominal imaging and CT are indicated if perforation or transmural injury is suspected. Early endoscopy, typically within the first 24 hours in an indicated stable patient, grades mucosal injury; defer unsafe endoscopy in instability/perforation and avoid casually instrumenting the later friable healing phase. Steroids/antibiotics are not universal prophylaxis for every ingestion; selection depends on injury grade and clinical context.

Early complications include airway injury, haemorrhage, perforation, mediastinitis/peritonitis and sepsis. Later fibrosis can cause long complex strictures, gastric-outlet obstruction and nutritional compromise; long-term cancer risk is increased after severe injury. Manage established strictures with nutrition and staged image/endoscopy-guided bougie or balloon dilatation. Record length, diameter and multiplicity; avoid forceful blind dilatation. Refractory disease may require selected stents/adjunctive therapies or oesophageal replacement, recognising that evidence and paediatric devices are limited. A gastrostomy may support nutrition and retrograde access in selected cases.

Diagnostic oesophagoscopy is also used for foreign bodies, dysphagia, strictures, bleeding and mucosal disease; therapeutic uses include extraction, dilation, haemostasis and selected fistula interventions. Perforation, bleeding, aspiration and anaesthetic/airway problems are material risks. Recurrent reflux after fundoplication may reflect wrap disruption/migration, slipped wrap, hernia, altered emptying or an incorrect original diagnosis; investigate anatomy and function before reoperation.

docs.title: Branchial anomalies, thyroglossal tract and cervical lymphadenopathy
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Branchial anomalies, thyroglossal tract and cervical lymphadenopathy

The first arch forms jaws/masticatory structures and is supplied by CN V; the second forms stapes/styloid/stylohyoid and upper hyoid components with CN VII; the third forms lower hyoid components with CN IX; fourth/sixth arches contribute laryngeal cartilages/muscles with superior/recurrent laryngeal branches of CN X. The fifth is rudimentary. First pouch forms middle ear/auditory tube; second tonsillar epithelium; third thymus and inferior parathyroids; fourth superior parathyroids and ultimobranchial contribution. First cleft forms external auditory canal; remaining clefts are normally obliterated. First-arch syndromes include mandibulofacial abnormalities; assess airway and hearing.

Second-branchial fistula commonly extends from anterior SCM skin, between carotid branches, towards the tonsillar region; cysts can present as lateral neck swelling. First-cleft anomalies may track through parotid/external ear structures and require facial-nerve protection. Third/fourth pouch sinuses often reach the pyriform fossa and can cause recurrent, often left-sided, thyroid/neck infection; endoscopy and imaging help define them. Treat acute infection first, then excise the tract or perform selected endoscopic closure with protection of nearby nerves/vessels.

Thyroglossal remnants arise along thyroid descent from foramen caecum. Midline swelling moves with swallowing/tongue protrusion; suprahyoid, juxtahyoid and infrahyoid sites occur. Differential includes dermoid, ectopic thyroid, nodes and other cysts. Ultrasound confirms a normal thyroid and characterises the lesion; thyroid-function tests/scintigraphy are selected when ectopic-only thyroid is possible. Sistrunk excision removes cyst/tract, central hyoid and a core of tissue towards the tongue base. Simple cyst excision has high recurrence. Treat infection before elective repair.

Neck nodes: I submental/submandibular; II upper jugular; III middle jugular; IV lower jugular; V posterior triangle; VI central compartment; VII upper mediastinal. Persistent suspicious nodes require history/examination, ultrasound, CBC and targeted infection testing, then tissue sampling suitable for suspected pathology. Avoid corticosteroids before diagnostic sampling of possible lymphoma unless urgently necessary. Sialadenitis evaluation includes hydration, oral/dental findings, ultrasound and duct disease; chronic cases may need sialendoscopy. Do not remove ectopic thyroid without proving adequate alternative functioning thyroid.

### Operative detail for branchial fistula and Sistrunk
For a second-branchial tract, mark the external opening, use a skin-crease/selected step-ladder exposure, follow the tract through its anatomical path and protect hypoglossal/glossopharyngeal nerves and carotid vessels. Excise to the internal termination when safely defined; dye/probes are aids, not substitutes for anatomy. In Sistrunk surgery remove the central hyoid with the cyst and tract en bloc and a core of suprahyoid tissue directed towards the foramen caecum. Recurrence is associated with residual tract, inadequate hyoid/core excision or prior infection. Confirm normal thyroid before excising a possible sole ectopic thyroid.

### First-arch associations
Treacher Collins has mandibulofacial dysostosis with important airway/ear issues; hemifacial microsomia/Goldenhar spectrum involves variable craniofacial and vertebral/ocular abnormalities. Pierre Robin sequence has micrognathia with glossoptosis and often cleft palate, with airway/feeding implications. Distinguish these developmental syndromes from first-cleft fistulas through the parotid/ear region; they are not the same lesion category.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [Duke embryology: craniofacial development](https://embryology.oit.duke.edu/embryoModules/craniofacial/craniofacial.html)

docs.title: Clefts, craniosynostosis, torticollis and airway lesions
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Clefts, craniosynostosis, torticollis and airway lesions

Cleft lip results from disturbed fusion of maxillary and medial nasal processes; secondary-palate cleft reflects failure of palatal-shelf elevation/fusion with each other, septum and primary palate. Assess feeding, airway, hearing and associated syndromes. Use feeding support and a multidisciplinary cleft team; primary lip repair is commonly in early infancy and palate repair later in infancy, with timing individualized to speech, growth and health. The historical rule of tens is not a universal modern prerequisite. Palatal options include von Langenbeck/two-flap closure, intravelar veloplasty and Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty; reconstruct levator function and achieve a tension-free closure. No single fistula rate is universally acceptable; compare severity-adjusted centre outcomes. VPI causes hypernasality/nasal air escape and is evaluated by speech assessment and nasoendoscopy, with speech therapy and selected secondary surgery.

Craniosynostosis is premature fusion of cranial sutures: sagittal/scaphocephaly, metopic/trigonocephaly, coronal anterior plagiocephaly/brachycephaly and lambdoid posterior plagiocephaly. Differentiate positional deformity. Apert (often FGFR2) includes syndactyly; Crouzon, Pfeiffer and Saethre-Chotzen are other syndromic associations. Assess vision, intracranial pressure, airway, hearing, development and genetics. Specialist imaging and craniofacial planning guide early endoscopic surgery with helmet therapy versus open vault expansion/remodelling; intervention aims at function and head shape.

Congenital muscular torticollis reflects SCM fibrosis; exclude ocular, vertebral, neurological, inflammatory and tumour causes. Ultrasound may show an SCM mass in infancy. Untreated tilt can cause plagiocephaly, facial asymmetry and scoliosis. Start stretching/physiotherapy and monitor; persistent fixed limitation/deformity despite treatment can require uni/bipolar SCM release, with postoperative rehabilitation. Protect adjacent nerves/vessels.

Congenital epulis is a gingival mass in a newborn; evaluate feeding/airway and excise a problematic lesion conservatively, with some small lesions observed. Subglottic stenosis can be congenital or acquired after intubation; grade endoscopically, assess airway symptoms and use selected dilation, endoscopic procedures, laryngotracheal reconstruction or cricotracheal resection. Large cervical lymphatic malformations ('cystic hygroma') reflect abnormal lymphatic development; MRI maps airway/vascular involvement, with sclerotherapy or resection selected by cyst type/anatomy. Plan EXIT for a predicted severe airway obstruction in a specialised centre.

### Repair methods and targeted operative points
Cleft-lip repairs include rotation-advancement (Millard), triangular-flap (Tennison-Randall) and anatomical-subunit approaches selected by cleft anatomy. Reconstruct orbicularis continuity, align vermilion/white roll and address nasal asymmetry while protecting future growth. Palate repair closes mucosa in layers and reorients abnormal levator attachments to restore a functional sling; a technically closed palate without good muscle function may still have VPI. For persistent muscular torticollis, release the restricting sternal/clavicular insertions with selected proximal release for a severe case, protecting adjacent nerves/vessels and followed by orthosis/physiotherapy; surgery without rehabilitation risks recurrent tilt.

docs.title: Surgical energy, laser, ultrasonic devices and CUSA
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Surgical energy, laser, ultrasonic devices and CUSA

Monopolar electrosurgery sends current from the active electrode through the patient to a return electrode; it allows cutting/coagulation but risks return-pad burns, coupling and remote thermal injury. Bipolar current passes between two tips, confining the circuit; advanced bipolar devices combine pressure with controlled energy to seal appropriate vessels. Observe each device's vessel-size limit and cooling needs; a seal is not assured merely because tissue was grasped.

Ultrasonic instruments convert high-frequency mechanical vibration into tissue cutting/coaptation with heat; there is no electrical current through the patient, but the blade can remain very hot. They can injure adjacent bowel/ureter/nerve by residual heat. CUSA means Cavitron Ultrasonic Surgical Aspirator: ultrasonic vibration fragments softer tissue with simultaneous irrigation/aspiration, facilitating dissection around firmer vascular/ductal structures, particularly in liver surgery; it does not eliminate bleeding risk. Argon/plasma devices and other ablative instruments have site-specific uses and gas/thermal hazards.

LASER is light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Wavelength, absorption, pulse duration and energy density govern penetration and thermal effect. CO2 is strongly absorbed by water and used for superficial precise cutting; Nd:YAG penetrates more deeply; pulsed-dye targets superficial vascular chromophores; holmium is important for endourological stone fragmentation. Applications include airway lesions, selected vascular/skin lesions and endoscopy. Use wavelength-appropriate eye protection, smoke extraction and airway-fire precautions; protect adjacent tissue and avoid claiming all lasers are equally safe for every lesion.

Energy complications include burns, delayed perforation, bleeding from an inadequate seal, smoke exposure, fire and device interaction. Inspect insulation/return electrodes, use the lowest effective energy, maintain visual control and keep heated tips away from vulnerable tissue. A good comparison states mechanism, intended use, advantages and particular limitations, rather than labelling one technology superior in all operations.

### Non-Wilms renal tumours and small-round-cell diagnostics

Infant renal masses include congenital mesoblastic nephroma (CMN), Wilms tumour, rhabdoid tumour and less commonly other lesions. CMN is common in early infancy; classic and cellular forms have different biological behaviour, with ETV6-NTRK3 fusions characteristic of many cellular lesions. Nephrectomy with complete excision is usual management; selected higher-risk/recurrent cellular disease needs oncology treatment and molecularly directed options. Monitor recurrence according to pathology/stage rather than assuming every CMN is benign.

Clear-cell sarcoma of kidney is aggressive and can metastasise to bone and brain; BCOR alterations support diagnosis in many cases. Treat with complete surgical staging and protocol-specific multiagent chemotherapy/radiotherapy. Rhabdoid tumour often affects infants and shows loss of SMARCB1/INI1 expression (or less commonly SMARCA4 abnormalities); search for synchronous CNS disease and predisposition. Pediatric RCC occurs more in older children, including translocation-associated forms; treatment differs from Wilms chemotherapy.

Immunohistochemistry is interpreted as a panel alongside morphology, site, age and molecular tests. Examples: RMS desmin/myogenin/MyoD1; neuroblastoma neuronal/neuroendocrine markers and PHOX2B; Ewing sarcoma CD99/NKX2.2 with a defining fusion test; lymphoma lineage markers; rhabdoid INI1 loss; germ-cell tumours SALL4 and subtype markers; hepatoblastoma hepatocytic markers with other morphology-specific stains. A marker is not perfectly specific, so avoid diagnosing a 'small round blue cell tumour' from CD99 or desmin alone.

Molecular tests can establish fusions, refine risk and identify actionable targets, using FISH, RT-PCR or sequencing as appropriate. Obtain tissue with a planned biopsy route and enough material for histology and ancillary testing; avoid necrotic tissue and inappropriate decalcification. Communicate treatment history because preoperative chemotherapy changes tumour composition. Liquid biopsy of circulating tumour DNA/cells is promising for residual disease and genomic profiling but remains tumour- and assay-specific, and cannot universally replace tissue.

### Bladder innervation, urodynamics and neurogenic bladder

Parasympathetic pelvic nerves (S2-S4) mediate detrusor contraction primarily via muscarinic receptors. Sympathetic hypogastric nerves (thoracolumbar) support storage through beta-mediated detrusor relaxation and alpha-mediated outlet contraction. Pudendal somatic fibres (S2-S4) supply the external urethral sphincter. Pontine and cortical control coordinate detrusor contraction with sphincter relaxation.

In spinal dysraphism, combinations of overactive/underactive detrusor and sphincter denervation or dyssynergia occur. Neurological lesion level alone cannot reliably predict bladder behaviour. A hostile bladder has unsafe storage/voiding pressure, poor compliance, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia and/or incomplete emptying that threatens renal function; a detrusor leak-point pressure near/above 40 cmH2O is a historical risk signal, not the sole treatment threshold.

Urodynamics measures vesical and abdominal pressure; detrusor pressure is their difference. Assess cystometric capacity, compliance (change in volume/change in detrusor pressure), detrusor overactivity, leakage, pressure-flow pattern and residual volume. Video-urodynamics adds reflux/outlet information; EMG helps assess sphincter coordination. Interpret against age, symptoms, infection, bowel status and technical quality. High filling pressure plus low compliance implies unsafe storage; low pressure with high residual suggests inadequate emptying. Demonstrate detrusor-pressure and sphincter patterns schematically.

After MMC repair obtain baseline renal/bladder ultrasound, renal function assessment and an early urological plan; urodynamic timing is individualized but should identify risk before renal injury. Reassess with growth, continence changes, infection or upper-tract deterioration. Clean intermittent catheterization ensures emptying; oxybutynin or another age-appropriate antimuscarinic treats overactivity/poor compliance. Beta-3 agonists and intradetrusor botulinum toxin are selected options when standard treatment is inadequate; dosing and approval differ by age. Alpha blockers target outlet resistance in selected cases. Botox blocks acetylcholine release; its bladder benefit is temporary and CIC may be required. Antibiotics treat symptomatic infection; avoid treating every asymptomatic catheter culture.

Manage constipation, maintain a catheterization plan and monitor kidneys, BP and growth. Refractory unsafe storage may require augmentation and a catheterizable channel. Priorities are renal preservation, safe low-pressure storage, reliable emptying, social continence and independence; a dry child can still have a dangerous bladder.

### Drug and pressure interpretation for a five-mark subpart
Antimuscarinics reduce involuntary contraction and can improve compliance, but cause dry mouth, constipation and sometimes impaired emptying. Beta-3 agonists promote storage-phase relaxation; confirm paediatric indication and BP effects. Botulinum toxin inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release and can be injected into detrusor for refractory neurogenic overactivity or into an anal sphincter for selected outlet achalasia. Its effect is temporary; reassess pressures and emptying rather than assume continence means safe storage. CIC is a drainage method, not a drug, and is often required alongside pharmacotherapy.

### Acute scrotum, horseshoe kidney, retrocaval ureter and urinary ascites

Acute scrotal pain has a differential of testicular torsion, torsed appendage, epididymo-orchitis, incarcerated hernia, trauma, idiopathic oedema and vasculitic swelling. Assess onset, vomiting, testicular lie, tenderness and inguinal mass; absence of a cremasteric reflex is supportive, not definitive. Colour Doppler ultrasound helps when available promptly but cannot safely exclude early/intermittent torsion in every case. Strong suspicion requires urgent exploration without imaging delay. Detorse, reassess viability and fix the viable testis and contralateral testis; discuss orchiectomy only for a clearly nonviable testis. Testicular salvage decreases with time. A 3-year-old still can have torsion; age must not dismiss the diagnosis.

Horseshoe kidney results from fusion, usually of lower poles, with impaired ascent because of the inferior mesenteric artery and variable aberrant vessels. It associates with UPJ obstruction, stones and infection. Ultrasound/cross-sectional imaging maps the isthmus and vascular anatomy before intervention. Treat the pathological problem; routine division of an asymptomatic isthmus is unnecessary. Retrocaval ureter is caused by anomalous IVC development, typically on the right, and can produce an S-shaped course and obstruction. Define the anatomy and function; symptomatic obstruction is corrected by mobilising/reconstructing the ureter anterior to the vena cava, with careful vascular protection.

Urinary ascites may follow neonatal bladder rupture, often with LUTO/PUV, or other urinary leakage. A distended abdomen, respiratory compromise and raised serum creatinine can occur from peritoneal reabsorption ('reverse dialysis'). Ultrasound, ascitic-fluid creatinine relative to serum and VCUG/cystography localise the leak. Stabilize, drain the bladder, drain significant ascites when necessary and treat the cause; some uncomplicated ruptures heal with drainage, while persistent/complex defects require repair. Renal dysplasia and obstruction still need assessment after serum chemistry improves.

![Original teaching schematic: neurobladder. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/neurobladder.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NCI PDQ: Wilms and other childhood kidney tumours](https://www.cancer.gov/types/kidney/hp/wilms-treatment-pdq)
- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

docs.title: Establishing and using a neonatal surgical intensive-care unit
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### Establishing and using a neonatal surgical intensive-care unit

A surgical NICU provides coordinated stabilization, operation and postoperative support for neonates with complex anatomy and limited physiological reserve. It requires neonatology, paediatric surgery and anaesthesia collaboration, trained neonatal nursing with staffing appropriate to acuity, nutrition/pharmacy input and access to radiology, cardiology, microbiology and other specialties. A room full of equipment without trained staff and escalation arrangements is insufficient.

Physical requirements include reliable thermal environments/incubators, space and power/gas supply, hygiene/isolation facilities and safe family access. Equipment includes size-appropriate airway/intubation tools, conventional and rescue respiratory support, oxygen blending/humidification, cardiorespiratory and temperature monitoring, infusion/syringe pumps, suction, resuscitation equipment and safe vascular-access supplies. Point-of-care gases/glucose and prompt laboratory testing, portable ultrasound/radiography, blood-product availability and PN preparation are important. Complex cases need clear access to tertiary interventions such as ECMO, rather than an assumption that every unit should provide every technology onsite.

Clinical protocols cover admission/triage, preoperative stabilization, fluids/glucose/electrolytes, sepsis and source control, analgesia, nutrition, catheter/device care, respiratory weaning, temperature control and safe transport. Use age/weight-appropriate drug calculations with checking systems and explicit handovers. Track fluid balance, daily weight and growth, skin/pressure protection and parent communication. Neonates with exposed bowel, CDH, EA, NEC or obstructive uropathy need different disease-specific goals within the common physiological framework.

Postoperative care monitors perfusion, ventilation, anastomotic/wound problems, pain and nutrition, while minimizing unnecessary invasive devices. Audit infection, mortality/morbidity, growth and neurodevelopment, with case review rather than judging quality solely by occupancy or bed numbers. Provide discharge training for stomas, feeding tubes or catheterization, clear emergency instructions and follow-up for development/hearing/renal function as indicated. A regional transport system needs trained personnel, warmed transport incubators, monitoring and an agreed receiving-team plan. The unit's purpose is prevention and early recognition of organ dysfunction as well as rescue after deterioration.

docs.title: VUR, UTIs and ureteric reimplantation
docs.body:
### Detailed revision answer

### VUR, UTIs and ureteric reimplantation
